The AfD won Saxony-Anhalt without migrant voters, but it cannot ignore them in Berlin.
items.titleTR: How Germany’s far-right AfD is courting the voters it promises to deport

slots.packetSpot:
Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt on 6 September, while the Christian Democratic Union remained at 17.2 percent. The party foregrounded policies aimed at limiting Islamic visibility through deportation and a “remigration” drive. Its programme also includes expanding detention centres for those to be deported, establishing a “deportation task force” and the possibility of stripping migrants who commit crimes of their citizenship. However, it needs the cooperation of other parties or elected representatives to be able to form a government in the state.

AfD is projected to win 18 percent of the vote in Berlin; 42.3 percent of the city’s population has a migration background. The party is trying to reach established communities of Russian and Turkish origin through TikTok and Turkish-language content; the message is built around the assurance that the problem is not established communities but newcomers. By contrast, DeZIM’s July 2026 panel showed AfD to be the party least likely to be chosen among voters with a migration background. In a 2025 study, AfD ranked third, with 19 percent, among voters with a migration background nationwide; it was stronger among people of Polish origin and ethnic German resettlers.

Arguing that “remigration” covers only the lawful return of foreigners without the right to remain in the country, AfD considers the deportation of German citizens with a migration background unconstitutional. By contrast, constitutional lawyers who examined the Saxony-Anhalt text assess that it points to a politics of exclusion based on an ethnic conception of the people. Similarities with Donald Trump’s political style and certain US policies also stand out; AfD’s affinity with them emerges as part of its search to broaden its voter base as migration policy hardens.

items.descriptionTR: GENEVA, Sept 17 (Reuters) - A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
items.titleTR: UN mission finds grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran, and Tehran crimes against humanity

slots.packetSpot:
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran reported in February that there were reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for two attacks on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab and a sports centre in Lamerd. The mission concluded that both attacks were indiscriminate and constituted war crimes.

According to Iranian authorities, more than 150 people, around 120 of them students, were killed in the attack on the school in Minab. The mission stated that the school was clearly a civilian structure and that it had found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes. In the attack in Lamerd, 22 civilians were reportedly killed or injured, while nearby homes and a school were damaged; US Central Command said it had not carried out an attack on the city that day.

The assessment, due to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, also concluded that crimes against humanity had been committed in the Iranian authorities' crackdown on anti-government protests. While noting that it had been unable to independently verify the death toll, the mission said official figures showed that 3,038 people had been killed and 25,000 injured. The White House rejected the assessment; US officials argued that military operations had been conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict.

items.descriptionTR: Yu became the youngest swimming world championships medalist in history last year when she won bronze as a 12-year-old as part of China's 4x200-meter freestyle relay team.
items.titleTR: 13-year-old Chinese swimming prodigy Yu Zidi cruises through heats at Asian Games

slots.packetSpot:
China's 13-year-old Yu Zidi advanced to the final after posting the fastest time of 2:07.97 in the women's 200-metre butterfly heats at the Asian Games at Tokyo Aquatics Centre. She was 2.7 seconds faster than the second-fastest time, set by China's Chang Mohan.

Yu won a bronze medal at last year's world championships with China's 4x200-metre freestyle relay team when she was 12, and also finished fourth in three individual events. In March, she also beat American Regan Smith, who has won multiple Olympic gold medals.

In the men's 100-metre freestyle, China's Pan Zhanle was the fastest in the heats with 48.07, while Japan's Tomoyuki Matsushita led the men's 200-metre individual medley heats with 1:58.56.
slots.packetTitle: Yu Zidi makes age irrelevant in the pool

items.descriptionTR: "We're putting stronger rules in place to keep Australians safe online," says Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
items.titleTR: Australian PM seeks big tech backing for internet safety, AI rules

slots.packetSpot:
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he was seeking the support of major technology companies for laws on children’s online safety and artificial intelligence regulation after meeting former Apple CEO Tim Cook at Apple’s headquarters in California. Albanese said they could not tackle online harms alone and that they were introducing stricter rules to protect children.

Australia last year brought into force a law banning those under 16 from accessing social media platforms. Draft regulations planned to be submitted to parliament during the year envisage imposing a duty of care on the companies behind major platforms and allowing users to switch off algorithms; consultations will first be held with companies, industry bodies and civil society.

Cook said Apple had shared new controls aimed at helping children’s online safety. Albanese also said new artificial intelligence standards would be introduced by the end of the year, drawing attention to the risk of AI developing in ways that could move beyond human oversight. He also said Cook viewed Australia’s social media measures as globally pioneering.

items.descriptionTR:
Critics say moves from leftwing incumbent president are electorally motivated two weeks before Brazil’s elections
Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced a 15% increase in the country’s main cash-transfer programme for poor families, as well as free weight-loss jabs, prompting criticism from opponents who say the moves are electorally motivated just two weeks before the presidential election.
On 4 October, the leftwing incumbent will face the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has been gaining ground in recent weeks.
items.titleTR: Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of election

slots.packetSpot:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has announced a 15% increase in the monthly payments of the Bolsa Família programme for poor families. The payment, set to rise from around £98 to £113, is planned to take effect on 19 October; that date falls just before a possible second round on 25 October.

Lula describes the move as an inflation adjustment aimed at protecting the purchasing power of the most vulnerable families. His opponents, however, argue that the timing was determined by electoral calculations. Lula's rival Flávio Bolsonaro called the decision “an act of desperation”, while Renan Santos applied to the electoral court for the increase to be suspended until the elected president takes office.

The programme covers around 50 million people, including roughly 27 million people of voting age; the increase is expected to affect 15% to 20% of voters. Although comparisons have been drawn with Jair Bolsonaro's temporary 50% increase before the 2022 election, views have also been expressed that Lula's adjustment is limited to inflation over the past four years and permanent, and that it is not, in principle, legally prohibited.
slots.packetTitle: Bolsa Família at the ballot box

items.descriptionTR: Ancient Chinese authorities used many creative ways to punish people, often with methods designed to mark them for life. One brutal example mentioned repeatedly in historical texts is cutting off a person's nose. However, archaeologists in China have never found skeletal evidence to prove that it occurred. But that may have changed following the discovery of a skeleton of a woman who lived in China about 700 years ago.
items.titleTR: Medieval Chinese skeleton may reveal first evidence of a brutal punishment

slots.packetSpot:
The skeleton of a woman in a cemetery containing 299 graves, uncovered in Henan in 2018, bears marks indicating that bone and tissue around and within the nose were cut from bottom to top. Radiocarbon dating shows that the woman, aged 40–45, died between 1298 and 1404, a period spanning the late Yuan and early Ming eras; healed bone edges suggest that she lived for years after the injury.

Chinese legal texts state that nose-cutting, cited as one of the Five Punishments, was prescribed toward the end of the Yuan dynasty particularly for the theft of valuable cattle or horses and for repeated theft of lower-value animals. Researchers say the skeleton may be the first known physical evidence of punitive nose-cutting in ancient China. However, disease, accident and self-inflicted injury are also among the possible explanations; it is reported that no signs specific to these possibilities were found.

Bony protrusions around the nasal opening may be linked to chronic inflammation or pressure from a possible artificial nose. The fact that the woman was buried face down, unlike the other burials, and that her diet was millet-heavy and limited in animal protein also draws attention; it has not been established whether these are related to the cause of the injury or to her social status.
slots.packetTitle: A severed nose, seven centuries on

items.descriptionTR: Some Western politicians are seeking conflict between NATO and Russia after a "failed" strategy to defeat Moscow in its war with Ukraine, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico ‌said Saturday. Longtime Slovak leader Fico, who has kept up warm relations with Russia and refuses military aid for Ukraine, said last week that Europe was ‌closer than ever to a large-scale war erupting from the Ukraine war. At the same time, some European leaders, such as those in France and Poland, have warned of Russian
items.titleTR: Slovak PM Fico says some in West seek war between Russia and NATO

slots.packetSpot:
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico argues that the strategy of defeating Russia through the war in Ukraine has failed; he alleges that some Western politicians are trying to shift the conflict into one between NATO and Russia. Saying that Europe is closer than ever to a large-scale war, Fico describes Western support for Ukraine as pouring gasoline on the fire.

According to Fico, the war in Ukraine is neither Slovakia's nor NATO's war. Warning that a drone violation could trigger NATO's collective defence clause, Fico says he wants to prevent NATO member Slovakia, which borders Ukraine, from being drawn into armed conflict; he says his country will not send troops on the basis of a fabricated pretext.

French President Emmanuel Macron, meanwhile, said that Russia had intensified its campaign of hybrid attacks against Europe, citing an attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in August, which the German government concluded was backed by Moscow. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also said, citing unnamed intelligence agencies, that Russia was planning hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine.
slots.packetTitle: Warnings from opposing sides of a NATO-Russia war

items.descriptionTR:
Simon Peter Carman appeared in a Pattaya court on Friday charged with killing Tunchanok Donhomla
An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty on Friday in a hearing in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, a court official said.
Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested in June after 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya City, about 150km south-east of Bangkok. A suitcase containing her body was found shortly after.
items.titleTR: Australian man accused of murdering Thai teenager and putting body in suitcase pleads not guilty

slots.packetSpot:
Australian Simon Peter Carman appeared before Pattaya Provincial Court for the first time on charges linked to the death of 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla, whose body was found in a suitcase shortly after she went missing in Pattaya. He denied the charges of murder, concealing a body and two counts of inappropriate conduct involving a minor brought by police and prosecutors.

According to police, Carman was detained at Bangkok airport in June while preparing to travel to Australia; CCTV footage from Pattaya shows him entering an apartment with Donhomla and later leaving alone with a large suitcase. It was reported that, in footage of Carman's police questioning, he said the girl had threatened him with a knife and that he had acted in self-defence.

Carman is being held at Pattaya Remand Prison. While the court's decision on whether the case will proceed to trial is awaited, a possible conviction on the charge of premeditated murder carries the possibility of the death penalty.

items.descriptionTR: Pat Brown won the vacant British and Commonwealth cruiserweight titles on home turf on Saturday night, counting out John Hedges in the sixth round at Co-op Live with a body shot he dedicated to Ricky Hatton.
items.titleTR: Brown delivers Hatton tribute after winning British and Commonwealth titles

slots.packetSpot:
Pat Brown claimed the vacant British and Commonwealth cruiserweight belts by stopping John Hedges in the sixth round at Co-op Live in Manchester. The 26-year-old Olympian from Sale won his seventh professional fight before the distance and dedicated the finish to Ricky Hatton.

The Harlow-born southpaw Hedges had been unbeaten in his first 12 professional fights. Brown was reported to have trained at the same gym as Hatton, while Hatton was reported to have coached Hedges and guided him to the English title.
slots.packetTitle: Two belts in a seventh fight

items.descriptionTR: Luke Littler threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at during his win over Nathan Aspinall at the World Series of Darts.
items.titleTR: Littler threatens Dutch boycott after boos and whistles in Amsterdam

items.descriptionTR: World champion Luke Littler beats Nathan Aspinall 10-9 to reach the last eight of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.
items.titleTR: Littler seals dramatic final-leg win over Aspinall

slots.packetSpot:
Luke Littler reached the quarter-finals by beating Nathan Aspinall 10-9 in the last 16 of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. According to the BBC, world champion and world number one Littler won the final two legs after falling 9-8 behind, finishing the deciding leg in 12 darts.

According to Sky Sports, booing and whistling directed at Littler overshadowed the match; referee Charlie Costorphine also intervened. Littler said he may not take part in European Tour tournaments in the Netherlands if the behaviour continues. He had previously refused to attend European Tour events because of the treatment by fans in Germany.

Littler's quarter-final opponent will be Jonny Clayton.
slots.packetTitle: Whistles in the shadow of victory in Amsterdam

items.descriptionTR: Nuno Espirito Santo's side were outfought and outclassed in the first half on Saturday. Their response after the break was impressive
items.titleTR: How West Ham upped their aggression and rescued themselves at Millwall

items.descriptionTR:
The Metropolitan police have been granted special powers to tackle violence as the south and east London teams meet again on Saturday after 14 years
Absence has not made the heart grow fonder. Millwall and West Ham meet for the first time in 14 years on Saturday, but it is not going to be a joyous reunion at the Den. The atmosphere will be ferocious and the main hope is that the focus is on the football rather than any nonsense away from the pitch.
These two have plenty of previous, even though they so rarely play each other. The most glaring example is the shocking disorder inside and outside Upton Park when Millwall lost in the second round of the League Cup at West Ham’s old ground in August 2009. A 44-year-old man was stabbed in the chest as trouble raged outside and riot police struggled to maintain order during the game, with play suspended briefly when home supporters invaded the pitch after one West Ham goal.
items.titleTR: Fear and loathing linger as Millwall and West Ham resume ferocious rivalry

slots.packetSpot:
West Ham and Millwall faced each other again after 14 years. According to the Guardian, the Metropolitan Police prepared special powers and measures to separate rival supporters because of incidents in the rivalry’s past; these measures do not mean that any incidents occurred at the current match.

In the rivalry’s memory are the stabbing of a 44-year-old man at the League Cup match at Upton Park in August 2009, police intervention and a brief stoppage of play because of a pitch invasion. The Guardian also writes that police horses entered the pitch after disorder caused by West Ham supporters at the match at Millwall’s ground in 2004.

On the pitch, Nuno Espirito Santo’s West Ham trailed in the first half; according to the Athletic, the effective response after half-time enabled the team to rescue itself. West Ham were top of the Championship on a four-match league winning run after beating Wrexham 6-0; Alex Neil’s Millwall, meanwhile, were 10th after an inconsistent start under the shadow of injuries.

items.descriptionTR:
Mohamed Salah scored a hat-trick and set up another goal as Trabzonspor ⁠thrashed defending champions Galatasaray ⁠4-0 at home on Saturday, handing the Istanbul side their first ⁠defeat of the Turkish Super Lig season.
Salah, 34, opened the scoring in the fourth minute, running ⁠through from midfield and finishing calmly, before he ⁠turned provider ‌to set up Noah Saviolo, who struck from inside the penalty area in the 39th minute.
Salah added a third in the 44th minute with a clinical finish from a Franculino Dju assist, sending the team he joined last month into the break three goals up.
He completed his hat-trick in the 80th minute, running more than half the length of the pitch unchallenged to score with a ‌trademark side-foot finish.
Galatasaray ⁠coach Okan Buruk was sent to the stands in the ‌71st minute while Lesley Ugochukwu was shown ⁠a red card in the 87th.
German ⁠coach Thomas Reis took charge of Trabzonspor this week following the departure of Fatih Tekke earlier this month.
Reis said: “First of all, we know Salah’s quality and what he is capable of. We know how dangerous he can be when he has the ball, but today the whole team fought incredibly hard. They fought incredibly hard to create those spaces for him.
“I’m very happy to be Salah’s coach. But at the same time, our defenders, all our midfielders, everyone did a very good job. Today they were very useful to him and helped him.”
Trabzonspor are fifth in the table with 10 points from six games, three points behind leaders Galatasaray.
They crashed out of the Europa League playoffs following a heavy defeat to Hungarian side Ferencvaros. Salah joined the Turkish club in the summer after nine years at Liverpool. He now has seven goals in six Turkish league games.
items.titleTR: Mohamed Salah scores hat-trick as Trabzonspor thrash Galatasaray in Turkish Super Lig

items.descriptionTR: The 23-year-old was returning home with a friend who got sick in the car when the Uber driver allegedly ordered them to get out of the vehicle on a California highway.
items.titleTR: Uber ordered to pay $40m to family of woman killed after driver left her on highway

slots.packetSpot:
In California, retired judge Richard Stone ruled after a five-day arbitration process that Uber must pay $40 million to the family of 23-year-old Emily Normandin-Parker. Normandin-Parker died after being struck by another vehicle following allegations that she was left on the highway after an Uber ride on August 12, 2023.

Her family and lawyers said the driver made Normandin-Parker and her friend get out of the vehicle at the side of the highway after the friend vomited in the car; both were intoxicated. According to the lawyers, rather than calling for help, driver Vu Tran called Uber and requested a cleaning fee. Stone said the driver could have used an exit to drop them off at a safe location.

Uber argued that the driver was an independent contractor and that the company could not be held responsible for his actions, and said it believed the arbitration decision was erroneous. The company said it had strengthened its safety approach over time, including driver guidance aimed at preventing passengers from being dropped off in unsafe locations. The family's lawyers also said that Uber initially offered a $10 million settlement on the condition that the family not speak about the incident, which the family did not accept.

items.descriptionTR:
Italian health authorities see evidence that rising temperatures and longer warm seasons are helping mosquitoes spread West Nile virus across a wider area, during more months of the year. ￼
Italian health authorities see evidence that rising temperatures and longer warm seasons are helping mosquitoes spread West Nile virus across a wider area, during more months of the year.
(Image credit: Gregorio Borgia)
￼
items.titleTR: As Europe warms, Italy sees West Nile virus spread

slots.packetSpot:
According to Italian health authorities, West Nile virus is appearing across a wider area of the country and during more months of the year this year. More than 650 infections have reportedly been recorded since the start of 2026, accounting for roughly half of cases in Europe; experts say the figure is broadly in line with levels in recent years.

Antonino Bella of the Italian National Institute of Health says higher temperatures can increase mosquito breeding and sometimes extend the transmission season until November. However, it is noted that the high number of detected cases may also reflect the extensive surveillance network monitoring mosquitoes, birds, blood donors and human infections.

According to Marc-Alain Widdowson of the World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe, warming weather will extend the period during which the virus and its vector can reproduce in more countries; nevertheless, climate change is not the only explanation. Biodiversity loss and changes in land use are also counted among the factors. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control had warned that longer, hotter summers, heatwaves and floods create more favourable conditions for invasive mosquito species.

items.descriptionTR:
With the repeal of a rule that limited carbon emissions from power plants, the president is further delaying the phaseout of coal.
Coal is by far the dirtiest of the world’s major energy sources. It accounts for almost half of the cumulative global carbon emissions since the industrial era began — as much as oil and natural gas combined. And it generates much more carbon dioxide per unit of energy than either oil or gas. Most climate experts agree that phasing out coal power is the single biggest change the world could make to slow down global warming. 
For almost 20 years, the United States has whipsawed on the question of whether the federal government should try to speed up that phaseout. After Barack Obama failed to push a carbon tax through Congress, his administration drafted the “Clean Power Plan,” which would have forced electric utilities to cut their emissions by shifting away from coal. President Donald Trump repealed that rule during his first term, and the Supreme Court later said that the president could not unilaterally force utilities to give up the fuel.
Instead of forcing utilities to abandon coal, the Biden administration tried to work around the Supreme Court ruling in its 2024 rule by giving utilities a choice. They could either retire their coal plants sometime in the 2030s, or they could equip them with new machines that would capture almost all the carbon dioxide that would come out of their smokestacks. The result either way would be a significant drop in carbon emissions from the power sector.
The Trump administration is now repealing that rule. The Environmental Protection Agency announced on Monday that it plans to wipe away all federal regulations for carbon emissions from the electricity sector, essentially allowing utilities to warm the Earth as much as they want. The agency used the same justification as it did in its repeal of climate regulations on motor vehicles earlier this year, arguing that the science of climate change was uncertain and that the repeal would save consumers money on power bills.
“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy,” said Trump’s EPA chief Lee Zeldin at an international energy summit in Texas. “We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America.”
This repeal deals a significant blow to the federal government’s efforts to force the power sector away from coal. The whiplash between Democratic and Republican administrations has been so frequent and so severe that neither the Obama nor the Biden rules have done much to speed the decarbonization of the power sector, especially when compared to other federal efforts like the Inflation Reduction Act subsidies for solar and wind.
“The reason to have a target is that it sends a clear signal to decision-makers in companies,” said Kenneth Gillingham, a professor of environmental economics at Yale University and an economic adviser to the Obama administration, where he helped draft the Clean Power Plan. “If you’re on the fence between choosing two things, you might as well choose the one that’s in line with the target. That’s been undermined. There has to be some teeth behind it.”
Even though the Obama and Biden rules never took effect, coal power has still been plummeting in the United States over the past 20 years. That’s thanks to the shale fracking boom, which lowered the cost of natural gas and made it cheap for utilities to replace their coal plants with gas plants. When burned, natural gas does warm the Earth, but slower than coal, and the shift has caused overall power sector emissions to fall in the U.S. by almost half.
The repeal of the Biden rule will likely delay that phaseout and will have significant effects for the nation’s public health. Coal plants also release harmful toxins like mercury and particulate matter, leading to thousands of premature deaths around the world. Inasmuch as the Biden rule would have sped up coal closures, it would also have prevented around $370 billion in health damages from climate change and air pollution. The Biden administration predicted that in 2035, the rule would have prevented hundreds of thousands of asthma flare-ups, hundreds of emergency room visits, and more than 1,200 premature deaths.
The artificial intelligence boom is also slowing the phaseout of coal. The Biden administration drafted its 2024 rule at a time when coal was expected to keep shrinking on its own; the rule projected a “continued decline in projected coal-fired steam generating unit capacity as well as a steady decline in annual operation of those [plants] that remain online,” driven largely by “eroding economic opportunities for coal-fired steam generating units to operate.” Now the rapid growth in power demand from data centers has led to a resurgence in demand for coal plants, and has led many utilities to push out the retirement date for their legacy coal assets. For coal power plants that sell into wholesale markets like the Midwest and the mid-Atlantic, high prices have made it worthwhile to stay online. (The Trump administration has also ordered some coal plants to stay online past their planned retirements, a move that a federal court found to be unlawful earlier this month.)
A case in point is Southern Company, the massive utility that produces energy for states including Georgia and Mississippi. Under the Biden administration, the utility had planned to retire its major Mississippi coal plant by 2028, but Southern announced last year that data centers would necessitate keeping it online well into the 2030s. The company’s previous efforts to install carbon capture at its coal units, meanwhile, have ended in failure. Environmental groups have criticized these decisions and argued that AI demand is inflated, but the Trump administration is happy to give utilities leeway to keep coal online.
The next president who seeks to take action on climate change will face much the same coal challenge that Obama did: how to speed up the phaseout of a fuel that is declining, but not dying? Gillingham argues that the short-term boost provided by Trump and the data center boom may not help rescue the coal fleet. The nation’s coal plants are only getting older, and many utilities will choose to replace them with gas or other fuels rather than repair them. The next president may still need the regulatory “stick,” but by that time the sector may be on its last legs.
“We have more electricity demand than we did before, which is, on the margins, going to make it easier for a coal plant to stay on,” said Gillingham. “But the trend is pretty clear, and you can only fight markets so much.”
This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Trump topples the last pillar of Biden’s climate agenda on Sep 14, 2026.
items.titleTR: Trump topples the last pillar of Biden’s climate agenda

slots.packetSpot:
The Trump administration is reportedly planning to repeal a 2024 federal rule on carbon emissions from the power sector. The rule gave power companies the option of closing coal plants in the 2030s or installing equipment that would capture nearly all of the carbon dioxide coming from smokestacks.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin described previous Obama and Biden policies as a “war” on coal; he said the administration was acting with the goals of more jobs, lower prices and the expansion of American energy. Kenneth Gillingham of Yale University said regulatory targets guide corporate decisions, and that this signal has weakened.

Electricity generation from coal has been declining in the United States for about 20 years, as cheap natural gas has replaced coal. But electricity demand from data centers and high wholesale prices in the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic are prompting some companies to keep coal plants operating. Southern Company, which supplies energy to some states including Georgia and Mississippi, is reportedly postponing the closure of a large Mississippi coal plant from 2028 to later years in the 2030s, citing data-center demand. The assessment that repealing the rule could delay the move away from coal and have public-health consequences is gaining prominence.

items.descriptionTR:
The US State Department has approved the proposed sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia for an estimated $24.3 billion.
The sale, which requires the approval of Congress, will "support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region", the State Department said in a statement.
It will “not alter the military balance" in the Middle East, the administration of President Donald Trump said, referring to a long-standing US policy that ensures Israel has a military advantage in the region.
Saudi Arabia said the proposed sale reflected the "strength and enduring nature" of its relationship with the US and existing defence partnerships. "For decades, Saudi-US security co-operation has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defence capabilities and advanced our shared security interests," the Saudi embassy in Washington said on X.
Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35 jets, the most advanced US fighter aircraft. But Israel, the only country in the region to possess the jets, opposed their sale to the kingdom despite a push for the two countries to establish relations. Israel has not yet responded to the State Department announcement.
News of the deal comes 10 months after Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman visited Washington, where Mr Trump initially said the US would allow the sale, while emphasising that Saudi Arabia is a major non-Nato ally.
Saudi Arabia is engaged in a conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, with the group launching several attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks. They have also seized Yemen's entire western coast, giving them unprecedented access to the Red Sea and Bab Al Mandeb strait.
The Houthis had reportedly been communicating with US officials to assure Washington that their latest advancements would not lead to attacks on American ships.
items.titleTR: Trump administration clears way for sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia

slots.packetSpot:
The US State Department has approved a possible $24.3 billion foreign military sale to Saudi Arabia that includes 48 Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II aircraft and 49 F135 engines, navigation and cryptographic equipment, logistics and weapons support. Formal notification to Congress has been made; Congress has the authority to review the proposal before final procurement contracts are negotiated.

The proposal is linked to Saudi Arabia's aim of strengthening its deterrence against drone attacks from Iran and conflicts with the Houthis in Yemen. However, Israel's status as the region's sole F-35 operator also raises questions about preserving the country's qualitative military edge. Reported possible assurances include equipping Saudi aircraft with less advanced configurations, software and weapons than those in Israel.

Some US lawmakers and analysts believe Saudi Arabia's defence ties with China could pose a risk to sensitive technologies. It is argued that, beyond military considerations, the sale could also serve a political function at a time when doubts are growing over the US security role in the region.
slots.packetTitle: Seeking balance in the F-35's shadow

The City of Ekurhuleni has dismissed suspended EMPD deputy chief Julius Mkhwanazi following internal misconduct proceedings, as he remains behind bars facing murder and corruption charges.
The City of Ekurhuleni has dismissed suspended EMPD deputy chief Julius Mkhwanazi following internal misconduct proceedings, as he remains behind bars facing murder and corruption charges.
items.titleTR: Julius Mkhwanazi fired by Ekurhuleni Metro

slots.packetSpot:
Julius Mkhwanazi, the suspended deputy chief of the Ekurhuleni Metro Police Department (EMPD), has been dismissed by the City of Ekurhuleni. The municipality had said that the suspension, which began on 11 November 2025, was an administrative measure intended to protect the integrity of the disciplinary process and did not amount to a finding of guilt.

Mkhwanazi is standing trial alongside five people on charges of murder, robbery and defeating the ends of justice in connection with the death of businessman Emmanuel Mbense. The Brakpan Magistrate’s Court denied their bail applications; the hearing was postponed to 24 November to allow the investigation to continue. Mkhwanazi denies the allegations; the dismissal decision is also described as a process separate from the criminal cases, which have not yet been concluded in court.

Mkhwanazi was granted R10,000 bail in a separate blue-light corruption case, but was not released because of his detention in the Mbense case. His urgent application to the Labour Court to halt the disciplinary process had also been dismissed.
slots.packetTitle: Dismissal in Ekurhuleni, cases still before the courts

items.descriptionTR: [Daily Maverick] South Africa has a 13th language, which saturates daily life and numbs society through its staggering brutality.
items.titleTR: South Africa: Violence Is South Africa's Unofficial 13th Language

According to the South African Police Service’s first-quarter statistics for the April-June period of the year, as cited in the commentary, 5,427 people were killed; 569 of them were women. During the same period, 1,052 people survived attempted murder. It was also reported that women’s bodies were found in the East Rand; among them was Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who did not return from a run.

items.descriptionTR: The former shipping tycoon was hand-picked by Beijing to run Hong Kong after the former British colony's handover to Chinese rule in 1997.
items.titleTR: Hong Kong pays final respects to former city leader Tung

slots.packetSpot:
A state funeral was reportedly held for Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive after the 1997 handover. Tung, who died on 8 September at the age of 89, was taken to Cape Collinson Crematorium after a ceremony at the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point.

According to reports, the ceremony was attended by Shi Taifeng, a member of the Chinese Communist Party Politburo and vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference; Xia Baolong, Beijing’s top official responsible for Hong Kong and Macao affairs; incumbent chief executive John Lee; and former chief executives Leung Chun-ying, Carrie Lam and Donald Tsang. Lee and Leung were reportedly among those carrying the coffin draped in the Chinese flag. Dozens of people from political and business circles attended the public vigil the previous day; residents were able to sign condolence books at three community centres until Sunday noon.

Tung was selected in 1996 by a committee appointed by Beijing; he led Hong Kong during the 1997 Asian financial crisis and the 2003 SARS outbreak. He resigned midway through his second term in 2005, citing health problems; the move was reportedly seen as linked to Beijing’s loss of confidence in him. While Chinese state media described him as “a distinguished patriot”, he is also remembered for governance problems during his tenure and public dissatisfaction that did not fully subside after the financial crisis.
slots.packetTitle: Farewell to Hong Kong’s first leader

items.descriptionTR:
Yann Bisseck believes Inter’s capacity to recover from difficult positions is now established, even if the performances that create those positions are not what they should be.The German defender sp...
￼
Bisseck reacts to Inter draw with Roma: ‘We know we can always turn a game around’
Yann Bisseck believes Inter’s capacity to recover from difficult positions is now established, even if the performances that create those positions are not what they should be.
The German defender spoke Sportmediaset after the 2-2 draw with Roma at the Stadio Olimpico, where Manu Kone’s first-half brace was cancelled out by two Lautaro Martinez goals.
“We are never dead, but we know that we can always turn a game around,” Bisseck said, with quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb.
He was clear, though, that the pattern cannot continue. “The most important thing is to improve. In these first games we are not always at our level, we have to grow and improve. Sometimes football is a bit strange.”
￼
ROME, ITALY – SEPTEMBER 19: Manu Kone of AS Roma scores his team’s second goal during the Serie A match between AS Roma and FC Internazionale at Stadio Olimpico on September 19, 2026 in Rome, Italy. (Photo by Paolo Bruno/Getty Images)
Bisseck on Inter’s slow starts: ‘Good question’
Asked to explain the Nerazzurri’s habit of falling behind early, he offered no theory at all.
“Good question, I have no answers because right now I am tired. I have to focus on the national team.”
He also played down the idea that Cristian Chivu’s half-time intervention was decisive. “Chivu does not have to tell us much at the interval, we know what we have to do.”
On Roma’s start to the season and their credentials as challengers, Bisseck was measured. “It is only five games, the championship is still very long. They are doing very well, but so are we.” He added: “We stay focused on ourselves and we will see what happens.”
The caution is warranted on both counts. This was the third Serie A match in a row in which Inter have trailed by two goals before recovering, a run that speaks to their resilience but also to a first-half problem nobody at the club has yet articulated. Lautaro described the opening 45 minutes at the Olimpico as needing to be wiped out entirely.
Roma, meanwhile, had won all four of their opening fixtures and conceded only once before Saturday. Gian Piero Gasperini’s side are level with Inter and Lazio at the top, and the fact that a two-goal lead against the champions felt like a missed opportunity rather than a bonus tells its own story about where their expectations now sit.
items.titleTR: Bisseck reacts to Inter draw with Roma: ‘We know we can always turn a game around’

slots.packetSpot:
Roma went into half-time 2-0 ahead at the Stadio Olimpico, thanks to two goals from Manu Koné. Serie A champions Inter made it 2-2 in the second half with two goals from Lautaro Martínez.

Inter had also come back from 2-0 down against Udinese during the week to win 5-3. After the draw with Roma, Yann Bisseck said they knew the team could turn matches around.

items.descriptionTR:
Barcelona secured an important 3-1 victory over Sevilla at the Ramon Sanchez-Pizjuan to keep their perfect start to the season intact.One of the biggest surprises from Hansi Flick last night, when the...
￼
Dominik Livakovic credits Barcelona teammate for helping him settle after impressive debut

Barcelona secured an important 3-1 victory over Sevilla at the Ramon Sanchez-Pizjuan to keep their perfect start to the season intact.

One of the biggest surprises from Hansi Flick last night, when the line-up emerged, was the decision to start Dominik Livakovic ahead of Wojciech Szczesny.

This decision came days after Flick revealed that the Pole was the second-choice goalkeeper this season.

The German manager later revealed that the decision to start the Croatian was a one-off and not a sign of the pecking order.

Livakovic enjoyed a winning start to life as a Barça player, with the team securing a victory and him putting in a decent display.
Livakovic delighted with perfect Barça start

As quoted by Mundo Deportivo, the 31-year-old spoke about his happiness after making his Barça debut and how Dani Olmo helped him settle in.

“We have achieved a perfect start to the season and we have to continue like this,” Livakovic said.
￼
Barcelona signed Livakovic to increase the depth and quality of the goalkeeping department. (Photo courtesy: FC Barcelona official website)

“There was a good talk at half-time and the team responded in the best possible way. We showed that on the pitch.”

Raphinha’s hat-trick naturally caught his attention.

“Congratulations to Raphinha, who scored a hat-trick, incredible,” the goalkeeper said, before describing the Brazilian as “the perfect striker because of the way he presses.”
Dani Olmo helping Livakovic settle

Livakovic also highlighted Dani Olmo’s role in making his first weeks at Barcelona easier. The pair already knew each other from their time together at Dinamo Zagreb.

“From the first day I’ve had Dani Olmo,” Livakovic said.

“I played with him at Dinamo Zagreb six or seven years ago. It has been easy because they are young guys and it’s like a family. It’s very easy to adapt here.”
￼
Dani Olmo helped Livakovic settle into life at Barcelona. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

However, the Croatian has not been the only one helping him.

“Also the goalkeeping coach, Joan and Tek are fantastic guys. Tek spoke a lot with me today, and so did the coach. They have made my job easy,” he added.

By signing Livakovic, Barça significantly improved the depth they had available in the goalkeeping department.

At 31, the Croatia international is very young for a goalkeeper and still has a few solid years ahead of him.

Both Szczesny and Livakovic know opportunities will be limited, with Joan Garcia the clear first choice, but it is always good to have back-ups of such quality.

With Joan expected to be back after the international break, Livakovic might have to wait longer for his next game in a Barça jersey, but his first outing was a largely positive one.
items.titleTR: Dominik Livakovic credits Barcelona teammate for helping him settle after impressive debut

items.titleTR: Raphinha hat-trick fuels Barcelona to 3-1 comeback win at Sevilla

items.descriptionTR: The EU laid out plans Thursday for strict age limits for children to access social media, games and AI assistants -- and on forcing companies to make platforms safe before minors use them.
items.titleTR: EXPLAINED: What would change for kids and social media under new EU law?

slots.packetSpot:
The proposal formally announced by the European Commission envisages restricting children’s independent access to social media according to age and imposing broader child-safety obligations on online services. Accordingly, access to platforms by those under 13 is planned to be banned; those aged 13 to 15 would be able to access them for one hour a day through “mini accounts” linked to a parent’s or guardian’s account. Only those aged 15 and over are envisaged to be able to open their own social media account.

The regulation, which is envisaged to cover TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat as well as YouTube, other video-sharing services, AI chatbots and online games, calls on platforms to comply with the principle of “safety by design” and submit child-safety plans. Companies that fail to comply with the rules could face fines of up to 6% of their global turnover.

Ursula von der Leyen said that the age limit would not exempt technology companies from responsibility for content on their platforms. The proposal still requires agreement among member states and approval by the European Parliament. Privacy concerns in age verification, how implementation will be monitored and the scope of the rules are among the issues under discussion.
slots.packetTitle: A new threshold for children online
