items.descriptionTR:
Constitutional Court rules that Shell and its partners failed to consult affected communities and did not properly consider environmental risks
The post South Africa’s top court blocks Shell’s offshore oil exploration right appeared first on Climate Home News.
After a five-year legal battle, the Constitutional Court of South Africa has blocked Shell and local partner Impact Africa’s permit to explore for oil and gas off the country’s East Coast, in a landmark victory for local communities and civil society.
“Today’s judgment makes me feel very happy and proud that the ocean is not for profit for mining companies,” said East Coast resident and environmental campaigner Siyabonga Ndovela. 
The verdict concludes a years-long process in which nonprofits Sustaining the Wild Coast, Natural Justice, Greenpeace Africa, and others took legal action against Shell, Impact Africa and the South African government for failing to consult affected communities – a legal requirement in the country.
South Africa’s offshore oil push meets grassroots resistance in court
The Constitutional Court ruled that Shell and Impact Africa had not complied with resource governance law, had failed to meaningfully conduct public consultation and had omitted to consider the impact on climate change, cultural rights, livelihoods and ecological harm. 
The ruling references last year’s landmark advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice, which states that countries have a legal duty to prevent and repair damage to the climate system. The South African judges argued that climate change “transcends borders” and states’ obligations “must be understood within the broader framework of international law”.
“This case must also be understood against the backdrop of well-documented struggles by coastal communities to protect their land, marine resources and ways of life in the face of extractive activities that they believe threaten their very existence,” wrote Justice Narandran Kollapen.     
￼
Protesters march to the Constitutional Court in 2025 (Photo: Ihsaan Haffejee/GroundUp)
The Constitutional Court found that the exploration right had been unlawfully granted by the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources. The ruling upholds a 2022 regional court decision against Shell and overturns a 2024 appeal that allowed the company to conduct fresh public consultations under the original exploration right. Friday’s decision means the right, initially granted in 2014, must be set aside.
Celebrating the ruling, Sherelee Odyar, oil and gas campaigner at Greenpeace Africa, told Climate Home News that the court confirmed “serious failures” in the awarding of exploration rights to Shell and Impact Africa, which “cannot simply be corrected later”.
The Wild Coast is a biodiversity hotspot that has been conserved over generations by coastal communities who rely on the ocean and land. “Our land and sea are central to our livelihoods and our way of life. Over generations we have conserved them, and they have conserved us,” reads the founding statement in the case. 
	•	￼   Aug 13, 2026  Nature   Will the world’s drying lands get relief from COP17 in Mongolia? Governments will discuss ways to combat drought and protect herders and their pastures from land degradation in a warming world  Read more    
	•	￼   Aug 12, 2026  News   “We’ve gone backwards” – new plastics treaty text dims hopes for production curbs During troubled talks, fossil fuel-producing nations have pushed for a global pact to tackle only plastic waste rather than reducing the size of the problem  Read more    
	•	
A Shell spokesperson said it noted the ruling, adding that “we are committed to responsible offshore exploration, meaningful stakeholder engagement and environmental stewardship.”
The Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources had not responded to requests for comment at the time of publication.
“Renewed strength” for communities
The ruling adds to a series of legal challenges brought by civil society groups against oil companies and the government as South Africa has expanded oil and gas development since 2014 under Operation Phakisa, a plan aimed at “unlocking the economic potential of the oceans”.
On the West Coast, Walter Steenkamp, chairperson of Aukotowa Fisheries Cooperative, which is involved in a separate ongoing legal action against TotalEnergies, said that “today’s court case gave me renewed strength”.
The case could also set a precedent for future oil developments, said Alessandro Mazzi, legal governance researcher at the University of Wageningen. He added that the verdict “sends a strong signal to investors that where projects affect people’s land, livelihoods and environment, meaningful consultation and genuine ecological assessment are an integral part of responsible investment”.
Janet Solomon, coordinator of advocacy group Oceans not Oil, said that the court’s emphasis on democratic participation, culture, livelihoods and the health of future generations in handing down the verdict signals a shift in jurisprudence on environmental governance, saying that this focus “may prove to be the judgment’s most enduring legacy”.
items.titleTR: South Africa’s top court blocks Shell’s offshore oil exploration right

slots.packetSpot:
South Africa’s Constitutional Court permanently cancelled Shell’s mining rights relating to its attempt to explore for oil off the Wild Coast. The ruling written by Justice Narandran Kollapen states that consultation with fishing and healing communities in Dwesa Cwebe, Amadiba and Sigidi had been inadequate.

According to reports, notices were published only in English and Afrikaans in isiXhosa-speaking villages; in some places, communication was restricted to traditional leaders despite objections. The court regarded consultation not as a merely formal procedure, but as a dignity-linked safeguard ensuring that those affected take part as equals in decisions concerning their own land and seas.

The case over the rights covering roughly 250 kilometres of the Wild Coast lasted nearly 13 years. According to the text, Shell had spent 1.1 billion rand on the venture; the court did not regard belated consultation as a remedy and declined to award compensation to the company.
slots.packetTitle: A voice on the Wild Coast

items.descriptionTR:
Venezuela has signed an energy agreement with France’s TotalEnergies, the latest in a series of deals with international companies as Caracas seeks foreign investment to revive its oil and gas sector.
Interim President Delcy Rodriguez oversaw the signing of a memorandum of understanding between state oil company PDVSA and a unit of TotalEnergies in Caracas on Saturday, her office said.
The agreement, described by the government as an energy co-operation pact, was signed by PDVSA president Hector Obregon and Francisco Javier Rielo, TotalEnergies’ senior vice president for the Americas. Details on the scope or value of the agreement were not disclosed.
Ms Rodriguez has said changes to Venezuela’s hydrocarbons law, approved earlier this year, provide a legal framework aimed at attracting new investment into the country.
Deal pipeline
The agreement comes amid a broader push to attract international energy companies after the removal of Nicolas Maduro as president in January.
Earlier this week, US oil producer Continental Resources signed a memorandum of understanding with PDVSA to jointly develop the Ayacucho 2 block in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt, one of the world’s largest deposits of heavy crude.
Other agreements announced this month include deals with Italy’s Eni and US energy technology company GE Vernova. The latter is expected to support efforts to modernise Venezuela’s electricity grid as the government seeks to rebuild energy infrastructure after years of underinvestment.
US company Chevron plans to invest $7 billion to double its Venezuelan production to 600,000 barrels per day over seven years, while North American Blue Energy Partners plans to invest up to $100 billion across 17 Venezuelan oil projects.
Venezuela has also opened up its natural gas sector to new foreign investment. Abu Dhabi’s XRG entered the country in August after being awarded a licence for the offshore Loran gasfield, becoming an equal interest partner alongside BP and Qatar’s UCC. The second phase of the project contains more than 4 trillion cubic feet of proven gas resources.
The deals come as Washington seeks a significantly larger role in Venezuela’s energy industry. US President Donald Trump has said an agreement with Caracas would give an American-backed venture control of about 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves, while also saying Venezuelan crude could be used to replenish the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
However, analysts say substantially increasing Venezuelan production could take years because of underinvestment and the cost of developing and processing the country’s extra-heavy crude. Questions have also been raised over the structure and implications of the US agreement.
Years of declining investment, ageing infrastructure and international sanctions have left Venezuela producing well below the levels reached at the height of its oil industry, despite its vast resource base. The recent agreements are intended to bring in the capital and technical expertise needed to raise output.
Venezuela holds about 303 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves, the largest in the world.
items.titleTR: Venezuela signs TotalEnergies deal in push for foreign investment into energy sector

slots.packetSpot:
Venezuela is continuing its search for foreign capital through an energy cooperation memorandum signed in Caracas between state oil company PDVSA and TotalEnergies E&P New Ventures. The text, signed under the supervision of Interim President Delcy Rodriguez, was signed by PDVSA President Hector Obregon and Francisco Javier Rielo, TotalEnergies’ senior vice president for the Americas; its scope and financial value were not disclosed.

Rodriguez said amendments to the hydrocarbons law adopted during the year provide a legal framework for new investments. A memorandum between Continental Resources and PDVSA for the Ayacucho 2 field, as well as arrangements announced with Eni and GE Vernova, are also among the elements of this direction. Chevron is reported to be planning to raise its production to 600,000 barrels per day with a $7 billion investment over seven years, while North American Blue Energy Partners is said to envisage investing up to $100 billion in 17 oil projects.

Despite Venezuela’s approximately 303 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves, its production remains below past peak levels. According to analysts, years of underinvestment, along with the cost and difficulty of processing extra-heavy crude, could spread any major increase in production over years. Washington is also reported to be seeking a broader role in Venezuela’s energy sector; Donald Trump had argued that an agreement with Caracas would give a US-backed venture control over roughly 65 billion barrels of reserves and that Venezuelan oil could be used for the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The nature and consequences of this agreement, however, are being questioned.

items.descriptionTR: Isaac Herzog grants request concerning former soldier Elor Azaria despite army saying he never expressed remorse, accepted responsibility
items.titleTR: Israel’s president clears criminal record of soldier who killed wounded Palestinian

slots.packetSpot:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog effectively erased former soldier Elor Azaria's criminal record by shortening the remaining period required for its expungement. Azaria had shot wounded Palestinian Abdel Fattah al-Sharif in the head in Hebron in March 2016; he was convicted of manslaughter by a military court in 2017.

Herzog's office said the decision was made following a request by Defence Minister Israel Katz in July, taking into account the passage of time, the completion of the sentence and the remorse expressed by Azaria, and that it did not reopen the original judicial process. Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir and other senior officers opposed the move, arguing that Azaria had shown no remorse and accepted no responsibility even 10 years after his conviction.

It had been reported that al-Sharif stabbed and wounded an Israeli soldier, was then shot by Israeli soldiers, and was shot by Azaria after lying on the ground for about 11 minutes. The 2016 shooting sparked intense debate in Israel and drew international condemnation; the Palestinian Foreign Ministry described the incident as an extrajudicial execution and a war crime, while the UN human rights office found the initial sentence excessively lenient.
slots.packetTitle: In the shadow of a criminal record

items.descriptionTR:
Police fired shots at crowds of migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on Friday in an attempt to move them from beaches to a new camp a kilometre away.
Six weeks after an estimated 80,000 people illegally entered Ceuta from Morocco, drawing international headlines and reproach from neighbouring countries about lax border controls, between 5,000 and 10,000 remain, putting additional strain on the city of only 83,000 people.
After a series of legal and political disputes, authorities were given permission by the National Court on Thursday to open a temporary camp in an industrial area of the Port of Ceuta, which can hold up to 1,500 adults.
About 150 officers took part in an operation on Friday to move them to the camps, sparking a crush. Police fired shots, injuring several people, El Pais reported.
The arrival of thousands of migrants over the summer caused a political headache for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has been accused of compromising the security of Europe by creating a backdoor to the continent.
￼
Ceuta is one of only two European cities on the African continent – Melilla, 225km away, being the other – while Morocco is a key partner for Spain on economic, counterterrorism and migration issues.
Italy and ⁠Spain this week extended the suspension of the European ⁠Union's border-free Schengen arrangement with each other for another 15 days. Italy said the decision was ⁠made because “significant risks to internal security persist, alongside a potential threat linked to possible terrorist infiltration”, the Interior Ministry said.
Mr Sanchez has insisted his government received no warning of the vast numbers who would arrive over the course of one weekend.
“No one could have anticipated the migration crisis that occurred on the 30 and 31 [of July]. No competent agency did. Not in Spain, nor in the EU,” Sanchez said in a post on X after declassifying a series of documents about the crisis.
Among the 40 documents and conversations released were alerts from July 29 about “a call to storm the [border] fence and come by sea”. They were circulated on Facebook and in WhatsApp groups with more than 180,000 members.
The communications from the intelligence services were passed to a low-ranking government official in Ceuta without anyone taking action. Those who were informed did not believe the threat would result in migrants arriving in such large numbers. And the warnings were not sent on to senior officials.
As a result, the release has triggered even greater scrutiny of Mr Sanchez’s actions and more questions about his accountability and competence.
For Spain's Prime Minister, the risk is that he miscalculated the degree of anger over the incident, including the ethics of going on a month-long holiday in the immediate aftermath and appearing to deflect blame onto Morocco. He also accused other EU nations of being “selfish” for not coming to Spain’s aid.
Opposition leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo of the right-wing People’s Party said the Spanish government was “incapable of grasping the true diagnosis and applying the correct treatment”.
“When a European border is violated, all of Europe is weakened,” he said. “When a border is not adequately defended, all of Europe is left unprotected. This is what is happening.”
He called for Europe as a whole to “acknowledge the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading and recurring”.
items.titleTR: Shots fired as migrants moved to new camp in Ceuta

slots.packetSpot:
A crush reportedly occurred during an operation involving around 150 police officers to move migrants remaining on Ceuta’s beaches to a temporary camp in the port industrial zone, with several people reportedly injured after police opened fire. The camp, whose opening was authorised by the National Court, has capacity for up to 1,500 adults.

It is reported that an estimated 80,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta over a weekend around six weeks ago; between 5,000 and 10,000 people are still in the city. Spain and Italy extended by 15 days the suspension of the Schengen arrangement that abolishes border controls, citing continuing internal security risks and the possible threat of terrorist infiltration.

Warnings of mass crossings are said to have circulated in Facebook and WhatsApp groups with more than 180,000 members, but were reportedly not passed on to senior Spanish officials. While Pedro Sanchez’s government maintains that it received no advance warning, Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo criticised the government and called for pressure from the European Union.
slots.packetTitle: The weight of the border in Ceuta

items.descriptionTR:
The American farmer, novelist and poet Wendell Berry, died on August 31 2026, aged 92. Berry farmed in Port Royal, in his native Kentucky, for over 40 years. Through his writing and his farming, Berry emphasised the importance of both community and care for the planet, advocating for small-scale agriculture as key for both.
He criticised modern consumer culture, suggesting, in his poem Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front, that instead of buying into the rat race, people should: “Love the world. Work for nothing […] / Say that your main crop is the forests / that you did not plant / that you will not live to harvest.”
His prolific output included The Unsettling of America: Culture and Agriculture (1977), Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer (1987) and The Mad Farmer Poems (2008).
Caring for the planet, Berry believed, means recognising your own place in it. Not as the centre, but as part of a wider community of interconnected life. In doing so, Berry’s writing highlights an important new theme in environmental humanities: a growing interest in “georgic” writing as an environmental genre.
The Peace of Wild Things by Wendell Berry.
The georgic is a classical genre that gets its name from Virgil’s Georgics – a long, four-book poem offering farming advice on ploughing, animal husbandry, fruit growing and beekeeping that was written around 29BC.
While for centuries the georgic was as popular as other classical modes like the pastoral or the epic, by the late 18th-century the form in English had all but disappeared, as the developing science of agriculture became more suited to prose treatises than long, complex poems.
Farming and environmentalism have long been pitched against each other. Over the 20th century, the worst excesses of industrial farming have decimated insect life in the US, as attested to by Rachel Carson’s environmental science book Silent Spring, as well as declining bird life in the UK.
Intensive agriculture has cleared vast swathes of the Amazon rainforest in Brazil and has been linked with the spread of diseases between animals, as well as contributing to antimicrobial resistance and greenhouse gas emissions.
However, since the 1980s, interest has been growing in agroecology and regenerative farming – practices which balance human and environmental needs. Often small-scale and community-led, these practices offer an alternative way of engaging in food production, with projects flourishing from Berry’s native US to Brazil, Spain, Australia and beyond.
In the UK, farmers are increasingly being encouraged to “farm for nature”, with grants available such as the Landscape Recovery scheme, the Sustainable Farming Incentive and the Countryside Stewardship scheme.
The georgic resurgence
This growing interest in balancing agriculture and the natural world is reflected in contemporary books and culture. In the last five years, there has been a growing academic interest in the ways that contemporary georgic writing might respond to environmental concerns.
The resurgence of georgic is in part due to a reimagining of what the form might be. It’s no longer just long, instructional poems that can be thought of as georgic.
Alongside farming novels such as Addlands by Tom Bullough (2017), or The Long Dry (2014) by Cyan Jones, poet Terry Gifford has identified three types of contemporary georgic non-fiction. These include “traditional instructional georgic”, like gardening manuals or the TV programme Countryfile, as well as memoirs, such as The Cow Book: A Story of Life on an Irish Family Farm by John Connell (2019). Finally, there is the genre of rewilding books, such as Wilding by Isabella Tree (2018), which Gifford terms as “radically future-oriented georgic”.
An interview with Wendell Berry.
Environmental humanities scholar Pippa Marland, meanwhile, has identified the “new georgic” – a genre in which farmers are engaged in producing nature itself. She cites English Pastoral by James Rebanks (2021) as a prime example.
While the term “eco-georgic” was only coined in 2011, Wendell Berry’s lifelong commitment to farming for nature and communities and to sharing his ethos and experience through writing, make him a fundamentally eco-georgic figure.
Berry’s legacy
Georgic is a didactic genre: it teaches readers things. Berry can be thought of as a georgic writer not because he wrote how-to manuals on ploughing, beekeeping or fruit-grafting (although he was a contributing editor at both New Farm Magazine and Organic Gardening and Farming), but because there is a fundamental quality about his work that seeks to teach readers how to coexist with nature and care for our planet, while feeding our communities.
In his poem Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front (1973), Berry asks readers to imagine our true crop as the trees that came before us and will outlive us. He urges us to think across the longer span of centuries. In doing so, he asks us to reorient our relationship with the earth. We should not see it simply as something to exploit and profit from. Instead, we should treasure it, even as we enjoy the crops and fruits that sustain us. Every reader, farmers and non-farmers alike, can learn from his broader ethics of care, attention and negotiation with the natural world.
Wendell Berry’s essay Think Little read by Nick Offerman.
Berry’s legacy, then, reflects a growing interest in agroecology over the past decades. But alongside his environmentally conscious farming, his writing touched many, feeding an appetite for ideas about how to live alongside nature, as much as for the food that farming produces.
The flourishing of the eco-georgic genre over the past decade testifies to a continuing and growing interest from readers and writers in a way of farming and living that cares for both nature and communities. Communicating these ideas is as vital as putting them into practice: making the pen is as mighty as the plough.
This article features references to books that have been included for editorial reasons, and may contain links to bookshop.org. If you click on one of the links and go on to buy something, The Conversation UK may earn a commission.
The climate crisis has a communications problem. How do we tell stories that move people – not just to fear the future, but to imagine and build a better one? This article is part of Climate Storytelling, a series exploring how arts and science can join forces to spark understanding, hope and action.

￼
Hannah Green does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
Every reader, farmers and non-farmers alike, can learn from his broader ethics of care, attention and negotiation with the natural world.
items.titleTR: Wendell Berry spent his life farming and writing – his legacy is an ethic of care for the natural world

slots.packetSpot:
Wendell Berry, the American farmer, novelist and poet who was reported to have died aged 92 on 31 August 2026, farmed in Port Royal, Kentucky, for more than 40 years. His writing and farming are remembered for an understanding that places humans not at the centre of nature but as part of interconnected life, foregrounding community, small-scale agriculture and care for the planet.

Works by Berry such as The Unsettling of America, Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer and The Mad Farmer Poems are associated with contemporary discussions of “eco-georgic” in the environmental humanities. This approach is considered alongside agroecology and regenerative agriculture practices that seek a balance between food production and environmental needs, holding that agriculture need not be in conflict with nature.

The long timescale that emerges in Berry’s poetry and essays suggests not seeing the land merely as a resource to be used for profit; it calls for attending to the world that existed before human communities and will continue to live after them, alongside the crops that sustain those communities. Berry’s legacy, having contributed to New Farm Magazine and Organic Gardening and Farming, continues to live on in interest in the idea of living and producing with nature.
slots.packetTitle: A voice for living with the land

items.descriptionTR:
The UN has passed a non-binding resolution to endorse the Equal Earth Projection, a map which more fairly represents the true size of the Earth’s landmasses. The current commonly used projection, called the Mercator Projection, greatly exaggerates land towards the north and south poles, which makes Africa look much smaller. In the Mercator projection, countries near the north and south pole can be anywhere from two to 14 times their true size. In the Equal Earth projection these distortions are minimised, making Africa look larger in comparison.
We asked Jack Swab and Derek Alderman, cartographers and geographers who study the social and communicative power of maps, to explain what’s going on.

What is a map projection?
A map projection is a technique that cartographers (map-makers) use to transform the round, three-dimensional Earth into a flat, two-dimensional map that we see on the wall or on our computer screen. As cartographers flatten the globe, the map becomes distorted, changing shapes and areas. There is no map projection that does not distort the Earth, but some projections are better suited for some uses than others.
A cartographer’s job is to choose from the hundreds of different map projections, and consider where the map is focused and how it is going to be used. No single projection is best for every use. This new Equal Earth projection is better suited than Mercator for producing global scale world maps for educational, public communication and policy purposes.
The Equal Earth supports a more accurate geographic understanding of the relative sizes of countries and continents. It provides a fairer perspective for the public to compare regions in terms of population, environment, development, politics and other global patterns.
Is the Mercator projection still useful?
While the Mercator projection isn’t good for showing the size of the Earth’s landmasses, we won’t see it totally disappear. For example, it’s very useful for navigational purposes as it maintains the accuracy of a compass bearing between two points without having to recalculate it.
This is why most online mapping platforms like Google Maps or Apple Maps rely on a variation of the Mercator projection to provide directions. Using the Equal Earth projection for navigation would not be as effective as the Mercator projection.
How will the Equal Earth projection be used?
Map-making is decentralised and there is no single authority regulating which map projection is used. What the UN did was endorse the broader message that Equal Earth is a fairer projection that more equitably displays the true size of the Earth’s land. And although this action is happening at a global level, there are movements underway in cartographic communities to make the Equal Earth projection the default world map projection.
The UN resolution by itself will not make Equal Earth a globally adopted projection. That requires intentional revision of maps used in textbooks, databases, media productions and diplomatic discussions, which requires labour and financial investment.
The Equal Earth projection was developed by cartographers and is a popular choice among map-makers since it was unveiled in 2018. It’s now possible to buy wall maps with the Equal Earth projection on them, and the projection has already been used in a wide variety of media. That said, individuals will need to opt in to using the Equal Earth projection over other types.
Why has the Equal Earth projection sparked resistance?
Resistance to the Equal Earth projection has been quite limited. There were several abstentions from the United Nations General Assembly vote, but most of this was for other reasons. Ukraine, for example, raised concerns over the depiction of the contested Crimean Peninsula on the map, which the Equal Earth Projection website depicts as contested territory.
This spurred a Russian response, along with points from other nations about contested territory. Given the UN resolution was a vote on how the world is portrayed and not about any specific political boundaries (a point that both Russia and Ukraine agreed on), these discussions amounted to geopolitical posturing about non-map issues.
The lone outlier, and only “no” vote against the Equal Earth projection, came from the United States. It claimed that the proposal was part of a “radical and ideological project” that was not appropriate for the United Nations to be debating. American delegates took issue with language linking Mercator’s distortions to colonial legacies and the marginalisation of Africa. This is not surprising since the current administration denies the existence of structural systems of inequality.
It is hard to miss the hypocrisy at play. The US wants other countries not to discuss the political implications of cartography even as President Trump engages in his own nationalist branding of the map. He has unilaterally renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America for clear ideological reasons and without international consultation.
How does the new map matter when it comes to changing global views of the world?
The argument that African nations put forward was that the Equal Earth projection is a form of “cognitive justice”. Cognitive justice recognises that people often equate power and value of places with their apparent size on maps. Traditional views of Africa as a smaller continent compared to Europe or North America typically reflect the perceived importance of these parts of the world.
Equal Earth may make it easier to teach, broadcast and discuss a different view of Africa and its prominence in the world. Today, African countries are among the world’s fastest growing economies and fastest growing populations. Map projections alone cannot change people’s attitudes. Yet, as African nations seek to have more influence in international affairs, correcting the mental map of global leaders is an important step in amplifying the continent’s relevance and rights.
￼
The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
Correcting the mental map of global leaders is an important step in amplifying Africa’s relevance and rights.
items.titleTR: New world map makes Africa look bigger: what’s the fuss about? Cartographers explain

slots.packetSpot:
The United Nations’ non-binding resolution supporting the Equal Earth projection has brought renewed attention to the debate over how world maps depict the relative sizes of continents. According to Jack Swab and Derek Alderman, every projection that transfers the globe onto a flat surface creates some form of distortion; the Mercator projection enlarges areas as it approaches the poles and makes Africa appear smaller than it is.

Equal Earth is considered better suited to more balanced comparisons of the relative areas of countries and continents on maps used globally for education, public communication and policy purposes. Mercator, by contrast, remains useful for navigation and wayfinding because it preserves compass bearings between two points; Google Maps and Apple Maps also use variants of this projection for directions.

The resolution does not make Equal Earth a mandatory or default world map worldwide. Changing maps in textbooks, databases, media productions and diplomatic use requires separate effort and resources. The projection, introduced in 2018, is reported to have begun being used in wall maps and various media projects.

The vote revealed that a seemingly technical map choice also opens up disputes over political borders. Ukraine voiced concern over Equal Earth’s depiction of the Crimean Peninsula as a disputed territory, prompting a response from Russia. The United States cast the sole vote against; its delegation argued that the proposal was part of a “radical and ideological” project and objected to linking Mercator’s distortions to the legacy of colonialism and the marginalisation of Africa. The “cognitive justice” approach advanced by African countries, meanwhile, draws attention to the possibility that visible size on a map may affect perceptions of places’ power and value.

items.descriptionTR:
The price of diesel in the US surged to a record high this week of $6.31 per gallon.
Diesel is still relatively cheap in the US compared with most other nations. But the rise will still affect a significant portion of the economy as it fuels logistics, operations and transport.
The continued rise of the fuel's price poses a major headache for economies around the world. With the situation in the Middle East still highly tense, crude prices continue to feel the pinch, with diesel facing a most uncertain path forward.
"Global diesel markets are under immense pressure. The Iran and the Ukraine wars have resulted in cutting the supply from refineries in the Gulf and Russia, making the US the crucial supplier of distilled petroleum products," analysts at UK bank Barclays said.
"This, in turn, has drained US domestic stockpiles ... given diesel's critical role in agriculture and the transportation supply chain, it will eventually add to consumer price pressures."
Felt everywhere
Diesel powers lorries, trains, buses, boats and vehicles in farming, construction and the military. Diesel-powered generators are also critical back-up power sources at factories, hospitals and large buildings, as well as in remote areas.
Diesel is derived from crude oil. But unlike the benchmarks Brent and West Texas Intermediate, diesel does not have a global exchange price. Instead, its cost varies greatly by region, influenced by supply and demand trends, logistical costs and local taxes.
Conflicts add to these factors. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, an ongoing flashpoint in the Iran war, attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi ships and infrastructure and the halt of exports from Russia amid its conflict with Ukraine are escalating supply concerns. The closure of the kingdom's East-West pipeline last week added to the pressure.
Supply disruptions, depleted inventories and increasingly high refining margins – the financial difference between the value of petroleum products sold by a refinery and the cost of raw crude used to produce them, which vary greatly depending on the components used – magnify a severe shortage of middle distillates, which is where diesel is classified.
Those factors have also caused diesel prices in the US and Europe to soar above $220 a barrel – about a 95 per cent leap from prewar levels, the International Energy Agency said. The price of diesel varies widely, with costs in oil-producing nations largely lower than in net energy importers.
Price increases vary in other areas but are still significant. In the Philippines, for instance, authorities are expected to announce a 9.50 peso ($0.15) increase in diesel prices, compared with a 5.50 peso increase for petrol, making filling up a vehicle to max capacity a substantial added cost.
US diesel is still cheap
Still, that places the South-East Asian nation in the bottom half of diesel prices globally at $1.363 per litre, according to data from industry tracker Global Petrol Prices as of this week. Twenty-four countries have prices below $1, including all Gulf countries, except the UAE, where it costs Dh4.30, or $1.17, up 13 per cent from August. Venezuela, Iran and Libya have the lowest cost at $0.004, $0.006 and $0.024, respectively.
At the other end of the spectrum, Hong Kong has the highest diesel price worldwide at $4.695 a litre – way ahead of second-placed Malawi, where it is $3.383. Sixteen out of the top 20 locations with the highest diesel prices are in Europe, including the UK, France, Germany and Italy.
The US, where the pain of higher diesel costs has already taken root – analysts warn of more if they remain elevated – is still in the middle of the pack with a per-litre equivalent of $1.66.
In China, where diesel costs $1.187 a litre, inventories of the fuel at state-owned suppliers fell to a 15-month low, prompting analysts to predict that Beijing may curb monthly exports to protect domestic supply – which would eliminate another key source of the commodity, especially for Asia.
But diesel has become "the bigger problem", said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Denmark's Saxo Bank. "The economic implications extend well beyond energy markets. Diesel is a critical input for road freight, agriculture, construction, mining and manufacturing, meaning sustained high prices eventually feed into transportation costs and consumer prices," he added.
Road ahead
The administration of US President Donald Trump has repeatedly said that high energy prices are a short-term pain, but the uncertainty over the Iran war's endgame casts a huge cloud over those promises.
The US Energy Information Administration this month raised its 2027 retail diesel price forecast by 8.2 per cent, referring to tight global distillate supplies and a domestic stash that continues to decline.
The Washington-based agency said in its short-term outlook that diesel would hit an average of $4.40 per gallon next year, which is a 33-cent jump from its previous prediction. For 2026, it updated its forecast by 4.4 per cent to $5.07 – before this week's spike.
"We forecast US distillate fuel oil inventories will drop below 100 million barrels in September and will remain below the five-year [2021–2025] low through much of 2027," the EIA said. "Tightness in the global distillate market has raised domestic prices and incentivised US exporters to increase distillate exports. We assume global production of distillate fuel will remain below last year’s levels in the coming months, contributing to low US diesel inventories and high diesel prices."
The International Energy Agency, meanwhile, said a partial offset for the diesel squeeze comes from other regions – amid disruptions in the Middle East and Russia – and inventories have so far played a "crucial role" in balancing the market.
"Gasoil and diesel exports from both the Middle East and Russia have been squeezed by the wars," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote. "With no end in sight, supply constraints will become a growing headache, especially as global oil inventories and strategic reserves have been falling. In other words, the clock is ticking louder."
items.titleTR: Diesel's record US surge drives more uncertainty for heavy-duty fuel

slots.packetSpot:
The price of a gallon of diesel in the United States has reached a record $6.31. The increase is being linked to supply disruptions reported to be connected to conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, declining inventories, tight global distillate supplies and high refinery margins.

Diesel is used in trucks, trains, buses and boats, as well as in agriculture, construction, mining, manufacturing and military activities; it is also a critical fuel for generators that serve as backup power sources for factories, hospitals and large buildings. For this reason, Ole Hansen of Saxo Bank warned that prices remaining high for an extended period could be reflected in transport costs and ultimately in consumer prices.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration forecasts that the average diesel price in 2026 will be $5.07 per gallon. The agency estimates that U.S. distillate fuel inventories will fall below 100 million barrels in September and remain below the five-year low for the 2021-2025 period for much of 2027. According to the International Energy Agency, diesel prices in the United States and Europe have risen above $220 per barrel.

•	Toby Samuel beats Andrés Andrade 4-6, 6-4, 6-1
	•	Wimbledon semi-finalist wins for 2-0 day one lead
Arthur Fery’s return to competition on home soil for the first time since his glorious summer at Wimbledon took place on a different surface, in a different format and on the opposite side of London. The emotions it generated were all the same as the British No 1 led his team to a 2-0 lead over Ecuador by defeating Álvaro Guillén Meza 7-5, 6-0 in Great Britain’s Davis Cup qualifier tie in the Copper Box Arena.
The victory for Fery, a Wimbledon semi-finalist, was preceded by a solid debut for the British No 5, Toby Samuel, a late injury replacement for Cameron Norrie. Samuel opened the tie by overcoming a nervous start to set the tone with a 4-6, 6-4, 6-1 win over Ecuador’s No 1, Andrés Andrade.
items.titleTR: GB take command of Ecuador Davis Cup tie on Arthur Fery’s London return

slots.packetSpot: Great Britain took a 2-0 lead over Ecuador after the singles matches in the Davis Cup qualifier in London. Toby Samuel, making his Davis Cup debut, won 4-6, 6-4, 6-1 against Andrés Andrade after losing the first set; Arthur Fery secured the second point by beating Álvaro Guillén Meza 7-5, 6-0. Samuel's victory, after he was selected following Cameron Norrie's withdrawal due to an arm injury, put the home team in an advantageous position ahead of Sunday's doubles. If the doubles does not produce a result, the tie will continue with reverse singles matches.
slots.packetTitle: Great Britain's strong Davis Cup start

items.descriptionTR:
Welcome back, then, the Dockers Derby. We really must do this again. On a lovely soft September afternoon on the Bermondsey peninsula, watched by an outrage-ready media multiverse, something unexpected happened at the Den. A really good football match broke out.
Not wild or violent. No shameful scenes that nobody (trans: everybody) wants to see. Not in the stands or the streets at least: the only really sour note was an allegation of spitting against West Ham’s Taty Castellanos, which will now presumably be investigated.
items.titleTR: Kanté and Mavropanos rescue late point for West Ham in derby thriller at Millwall

slots.packetSpot: The Dockers Derby at The Den in Bermondsey ended 2-2. Millwall went 2-0 up through goals from Caleb Taylor and Camiel Neghli; West Ham levelled the score through N’Golo Kanté and Konstantinos Mavropanos. In a match in which no violence was reported in the stands or on the streets, an allegation that West Ham forward Taty Castellanos spat at Millwall goalkeeper Filip Marschall came to the fore; it was stated that the allegation was expected to be investigated.
slots.packetTitle: A shadow over a quiet derby

Supporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empire
Manchester United’s Muslim supporters’ Club (MUMSC) has called for the Premier League side’s co-owner to step down after he made “completely unacceptable” comments during a BBC interview.
Sir Jim Ratcliffe described the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world”.
items.titleTR: Manchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quit

slots.packetSpot:
Manchester United Muslim Supporters’ Club called for co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to step down, describing his remarks on the United Kingdom, empire, immigration and welfare as “completely unacceptable”. The text posted on X, described as a “statement of no confidence”, also called for the Glazer family to leave the club.

In an interview with the BBC, Ratcliffe said the United Kingdom was “in decline”; he had expressed his views on high taxes, wealth and immigration. The supporters’ club said it had previously objected to Ratcliffe’s remarks earlier this year that the country was “being colonised by immigrants”.

Tensions between Ratcliffe and some Manchester United supporters are also continuing over ticket prices, the dismissal of 450 club employees and the cancellation of 685 season tickets.

￼The "Great Mosaic" may be the largest in the Roman world.

￼
At 33 feet wide and 52.5 feet high, an ancient mosaic recently unveiled to the public may be the largest in the entire Roman world. It sits within the recently opened Museum of the Baths of Trajan in central Rome, which preserves a monumental, early 2nd-century bath complex built by Emperor Trajan covering about 15 acres.
To construct the baths on the Oppian Hill, builders repurposed elements of a previous structure, Emperor Nero’s Domus Aurea, or “Golden House,” originally erected between 64 and 68 C.E. It’s unclear if the mosaic originated in that building; archaeologists think it could have also been part of a lavish dwelling that was later incorporated into the compound. But many of the monumental composition’s tesserae are missing and may have been used in the construction of the baths.
￼
Dubbed the “Great Mosaic,” the work was discovered in 2011, and archaeologists have been meticulously revealing and conserving it since. The in situ artwork depicts architectural features that may represent a dual-level theatrical set, known as a scaenae frons, plus statues of the Muses and other figures and patterns that mimic the appearance of marble.
Within the same complex, a remarkable architectural fresco uncovered in the 1990s also goes on view for the first time. Known as the “Painted City,” it’s unclear whether the scenic backdrop for bathers depicts an actual port city or an imaginary place. According to CNN, the aerial perspective portrays some unusual details such as public squares and towers that weren’t a common feature of municipal design in the 1st century.
Archaeologists continue to excavate the “Great Mosaic,” particularly an area focusing on wine-making and grapes. Much of it can now be seen by visitors from an elevated walkway.

slots.packetSpot:
It was reported that the “Muse and Philosopher” mosaic and the “Painted City” fresco, found during excavations in the 1990s in the underground gallery beneath the Baths of Trajan in Rome, have been opened to visitors at weekends. The first visits were said to have taken place on 12–13 September, in groups of 15; from 2 October, visits were stated to continue between Friday and Sunday.

Of the works thought to date to the first century, the fresco depicts a harbour city seen from above, with its walls and towers. The mosaic, 10 metres high and extending 16 metres along the wall, contains a theatrical scene featuring figures, architectural structures, statues and real people. Archaeologist Francesco Pacetti said they estimate that the mosaic may be the largest wall mosaic found in the Roman world to date.

Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri wrote that the fresco may belong to the Neronian or Flavian period, and therefore predate the Baths of Trajan, which opened in 109. An on-site museum focused on the baths also opened at the beginning of the month; it was stated that the restoration was carried out under the €500 million PNRR-Caput Mundi programme financed by the European Union.
slots.packetTitle: A city uncovered beneath the Baths of Trajan

But the military's overall use of AI seems to be accelerating.
The US narrowly avoided boarding a Chinese ship based on an "entirely false" US intelligence report generated with the help of AI tools, according to a CNN report.
That erroneous intelligence, submitted by a US Special Operations Command analyst, suggested the Chinese ship was transporting nuclear arms program components through the Middle East, according to "four sources familiar with the episode" cited by CNN. The US military was preparing to intercept and board the ship, with air support, before officials discovered a chatbot used in generating the report had "inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying."
One source told CNN the AI-powered fiasco "almost started a war."

Researchers used Claude to reach an OpenAI employee account and sensitive GitHub data.
Cyber researchers broke into OpenAI using its key rival Anthropic’s software, highlighting vulnerabilities in the ChatGPT maker’s security as leading AI companies face mounting scrutiny over safety.
A small cyber security group gained access to an OpenAI employee’s ChatGPT account, which permitted them to read private software information and suggest changes.
The researchers had been given access to an Anthropic tool specifically designed for security professionals, and were paid for the work as part of a program to find vulnerabilities before they could be exploited by bad actors.

items.descriptionTR: The hacking ability of AI is leading Beijing to see threats in a new light, with its spy agency warning that national security could be in danger.
items.titleTR: AI ‘warning shots’ focus Beijing on national security risks

slots.packetSpot:
AI’s effects on security are becoming apparent in a range of risks, from military intelligence to the systems of major technology companies and national security assessments.

According to CNN, citing four sources with knowledge of the matter, an intelligence report prepared by an analyst at U.S. Special Operations Command with the help of AI tools mistakenly identified material aboard a Chinese ship as components belonging to a nuclear weapons program. Before the error came to light, the U.S. military was preparing to stop the ship with air support and board it. One of the sources said the incident “almost started a war.”

In a separate security study, researchers used Anthropic’s Claude tool for security experts to gain access to an OpenAI employee’s ChatGPT account and sensitive GitHub software information. The study was conducted under a program in which researchers are paid to identify vulnerabilities before they can be exploited by malicious actors.

China’s intelligence agency, meanwhile, warned that AI’s hacking capacity could endanger national security. The warning indicates that Beijing is assessing AI-enabled cyber threats through a different framework.
slots.packetTitle: The security gaps opened by AI

items.descriptionTR: As Russia increases its attacks on Ukraine's rail infrastructure, the Ukrainian government has called for help to replace destroyed locomotives and is making plans to keep passengers safe.
items.titleTR: Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways

items.descriptionTR:
￼
In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up drone strikes on Ukraine's rail network, targeting trains and the approximately 20,000 kilometres of track that form a key transportation artery across the country.
items.titleTR: Russian drones are stalking Ukrainian trains and trying to hobble the country's rail system

slots.packetSpot:
Russia’s drone attacks on Ukraine’s trains, locomotives and railway infrastructure are continuing. According to Ukrzaliznytsia official Oleh Holovashchenko, more than 1,600 attacks were reported in the first eight months of 2026; officials cited by CBC say that about 300 locomotives and 120 passenger carriages have been hit this year.

The railway remains a critical line for evacuations, aid, grain and other goods, as well as passenger transport. While the attacks have caused delays and evacuations, new rules have also been introduced limiting passengers’ ability to board or leave trains during air-raid alerts. According to CBC, two dozen railway workers have been killed and more than 80 injured this year; at least one person was also killed and seven injured in a drone attack on a train in the Kharkiv region.

Russia’s Foreign Ministry considers railway hubs serving the Ukrainian military to be legitimate targets; other Russian officials argue that the attacks are directed at infrastructure linked to military cargo from Europe. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, describes the attacks as part of a strategy to weaken the economy and disrupt daily life.

Ukraine is seeking to strengthen protection through monitoring and early-warning systems, preventive stops, bus connections, electronic warfare assets, mobile fire teams and air-defence lines. Repairs to damaged vehicles are continuing, while Ukrzaliznytsia is in talks with international partners to procure new locomotives; locomotives covered by a contract signed with France’s Alstom are planned to arrive next year.
slots.packetTitle: Railway under the pressure of war

items.titleTR: US embassies issue security alerts over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

items.titleTR: Turkiye backs Saudi Arabia’s security amid escalating Houthi attacks: FM

slots.packetSpot:
Yemen’s Iran-linked Houthi movement claimed to have carried out two operations targeting sensitive sites in Riyadh and Aramco facilities in Yanbu, using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones. A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition confirmed that a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh had been intercepted by air defences; he said Baish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu had also been targeted. Flames and smoke were reportedly seen near King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh; Flightradar24 said the airport was experiencing major problems.

US embassies in the Middle East called on Americans to exercise greater caution, assessing that the security environment remained complex and that military conflict had the potential to escalate rapidly. The warnings also drew attention to possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saudi Arabia may have military needs, particularly in technical fields, and that Turkey would consider meeting those needs under the trilateral defence agreement to which it is a party alongside Pakistan. Fidan also said Saudi Arabia should not be drawn into the US-Iran war. Pakistan, too, committed to defending Saudi Arabia under the agreement.

According to the UN, 110 civilian casualties were documented in 31 incidents in Taiz, Hudaydah and Marib since the escalation of fighting in August, including 28 people killed and 82 injured. It was stated that the real number was likely to be higher because of security and access restrictions.

items.descriptionTR: Parliament speaker says Tehran has conveyed conditions through intermediaries, rules out reopening strategic waterway until they are met
items.titleTR: Iran says Strait of Hormuz to remain closed until US fulfills commitments

items.descriptionTR: Iran says it struck an oil tanker that was attempting to “illegally pass” through the Strait of Hormuz.  Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said in a statement shared by state media that it attacked a Togo-flagged tanker, the Trend, after it tried to navigate through the waterway.  The vessel “came to a halt after catching fire,” according…
items.titleTR: Iran says it struck oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz

slots.packetSpot:
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the Strait of Hormuz could reopen if the United States fulfils its commitments under the June agreement and conditions that Tehran says it conveyed through mediators are met. According to Ghalibaf, the agreement, which included provisions to halt military operations and reopen the strait to maritime traffic, later collapsed because of disputes over navigation and security.

In a statement carried by state media, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they struck the Togolese-flagged tanker Trend, which they alleged was attempting to pass through the strait illegally, and reported that the vessel came to a halt after catching fire. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre announced that a security incident had occurred 16 nautical miles off Khasab, Oman, that the crew was safe and that no environmental impact had been reported; whether this incident was connected to the tanker attack reported by Iran remained unclear.

The strait, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's daily oil consumption normally passes, is reported to have been effectively closed since military operations between the United States and Iran began in late February.

items.descriptionTR:
The conflict between Iran and the US appears to have reached a stalemate. The US navy continues to prevent Iranian vessels or others transiting to or from Iranian ports. Iran, meanwhile, threatens shipping moving in or out of the Persian Gulf region via the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has also recently said it will establish a new “restricted zone” stretching into the Gulf from the Strait of Hormuz – although details remain sketchy.
Less frequently discussed is the network of undersea cables across the Persian Gulf which connect the region with the outside world. On August 16, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Iranian government was considering attacks on that network. In the Gulf’s relatively shallow waters, threats to this critical undersea infrastructure (CUI) pose a credible risk to the Gulf States and the wider world.
These cables form a largely unseen foundation of the global economy, carrying more than 95% of international data traffic. Their role extends far beyond everyday internet and call usage. They support financial transactions, government communications and the increasingly data-intensive operations of the global technology sector.
Major technology companies such as Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are investing heavily in subsea connectivity as they expand data-centre networks and seek to meet the growing demands of AI. For the Gulf States, where hundreds of billions of dollars are being invested in AI as part of efforts to diversify economies away from fossil fuels, disruption to this infrastructure could therefore have consequences far beyond communications. Cutting these CUI cables threatens a key element of their broader economic ambitions.
To demonstrate the scale of this risk, the key cable networks include the Fibre in Gulf submarine cable system, which connects Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE. There is also the Falcon Network, which connects Bahrain, Egypt, India, Iraq, Kuwait, Maldives, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Sudan and Yemen. The Asia-Africa-Europe1 (AEE1) network, with landing sites in Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE, linking southeast Asia to Europe via Egypt. And the Gulf Bridge International, which links Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and has onward connectivity to India and Europe.
￼
Key undersea internet calbes are vulnerale to disruption in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. TeleGeography, CC BY-NC-SA
With that web of connections funnelled through the Strait of Hormuz, an international waterway that has long been of strategic importance for oil and gas has taken on a new significance as a choke point for global undersea infrastructure.
What makes the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Gulf region particularly vulnerable to an attack on the CUI is the shallow water. With an average depth of 50 metres and a maximum depth of less than 100 metres, those who might wish to attack the CUI network do not need the sort of high-end capabilities of Russia’s Gugi agency. Gugi, which is the Russian acronym for the Main Directorate of Deep Sea Research, is responsible for underwater sabotage and espionage.
Remotely operated vehicles (ROV) with working depths of thousands of metres are commonplace in the oil and gas industry. There are growing numbers of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUV) with similar operating parameters in that field. Both can be repurposed and used for offensive operations.
Iran has already debuted its own mine clearance ROV, and there may be other capabilities which it has not chosen to publicise. The shallowness of the Persian Gulf puts most of it well within the depths military divers are able to operate at. We could also see the sort of blunt threat posed by a ship “accidentally” dragging its anchor to cut cables in the manner we have witnessed in the Baltic.
So it’s entirely feasible that Iran could conduct attacks against the CUI network. And the threat has already affected planned extensions or new elements of this undersea infrastructure. Several projects have been put on hold after their owners or contractors declared they can’t safely operate in the Gulf.
This neatly illustrates the impact of conflict on the ability to maintain and extend the cables carrying so much of the world’s trade and communication. In the context of the Middle East, that will have a direct impact on the ambitions of Gulf States to become AI-enabled economies.
Iran clearly appreciates the strategic and operational significance of the regional CUI network and will have put significant effort into mapping it. It is also reasonable to assume that it will have a trained force of divers able to operate at depths that would enable them to reach the cables across the Persian Gulf seabed.
We know that they have an ROV designed for mine clearance operations – and it’s highly likely operate other assets in support of a well-developed offshore oil industry.
How far would Iran go?
The most important question is what would the Iranians be prepared to do? An attack on the cable network could create a very significant impact on trade and communications across the Middle East, with global ramifications. Such an attack would need to be targeted and limited if Iran wished to avoid global condemnation. But it’s a risk they may be willing to take given their current isolation.
That “maybe-they-would” doubt leads us to consider a new form of deterrence – of one nation’s ability to affect either CUI of another, or of broader networks.
It’s something of an extension of Nixon’s madman theory of nuclear deterrence. A nation that is desperate enough could be willing to take extreme action in the CUI domain – with what might appear to a rational observer to be disproportionate regional and potentially global consequences – in order to deter more traditional military strikes against it.
To a certain extent this should come as no surprise. The CUI network is the cyber age equivalent of the roads, bridges and rail systems which have long been targets for military planners seeking to disrupt an opponents’ ability and willingness to fight. Iran’s capacity and desire to conduct this sort of operation may be uncertain – but that very ambiguity may prove enough to have a significant impact on the region.
￼
John Aitken does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

items.descriptionTR: Countries and companies are investing in technologies for underwater use amid concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure on the ocean floor.
items.titleTR: A new arms race is unfolding on the ocean floor

slots.packetSpot:
The possibility of a potential attack on submarine cables around the Strait of Hormuz is once again bringing into focus just how fragile seabed infrastructure is. According to the Wall Street Journal on 16 August, the Iranian government was considering attacking this network in the Persian Gulf; however, Iran’s capacity and intent remain unclear.

The cables in the region are important not only for communications and financial transactions, but also for public activities and the Gulf countries’ AI-focused economic plans. Shallow waters increase the risk of interference through remotely operated or autonomous underwater vehicles and divers; it is also stated that some cable projects have been postponed for security reasons.

This vulnerability is accelerating investment by states and companies in subsea surveillance, sensors, autonomous vehicles and underwater communications. According to TeleGeography, more than 1.5 million kilometres of submarine communications cable were in service worldwide as of early 2026. Even so, it does not appear realistic for autonomous systems to protect every line on the seabed: the technical obstacles are substantial, while responsibility remains unclear between infrastructure owners and governments.
slots.packetTitle: The fault line beneath the sea

items.titleTR: Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron

items.descriptionTR: A series of sabotage attacks in the EU all point back to Russia. Now the EU has to decide how to respond. A series of sabotage attacks in the EU all point back to Russia. Now the EU has to decide how to respond.
items.titleTR: ARTE Europe Weekly: When Does a Hybrid War Become a Real War?

items.descriptionTR: Serbia and Montenegro are hosting crucial nodes in the complex infrastructure of Russian cybercrime and disinformation operations in Europe, according to the findings of a BIRN investigation. Serbia and Montenegro are hosting crucial nodes in the complex infrastructure of Russian cybercrime and disinformation operations in Europe, according to the findings of a BIRN investigation.
items.titleTR: ‘Disposable’ IP Firms in Serbia, Montenegro Obscure Origins of Russian Cyber Meddling

slots.packetSpot:
Hybrid pressure allegedly linked to Russia in Europe is being treated as an issue extending from physical security to digital infrastructure. Macron said France had been targeted in recent weeks and called for a plan to protect critical infrastructure and sensitive defence and technology facilities against drone and cyberattacks. Other warnings in Europe also point to possible drone and missile attacks intended to test support for Ukraine; accusations directed at Russia over a drone attack near Leipzig Airport and suspicious fires at defence facilities are reported in this context.

The increase in acts of sabotage on EU territory is deepening the debate over whether this can still be called “hybrid warfare” and how deterrence can be established without creating a risk of escalation.

A technical review of certain companies, individuals and IP ranges in Serbia and Montenegro states that digital networks linked to sanctioned Russian providers intersect with infrastructure used in cybercrime, cyberattacks, influence and disinformation activities. These links alone do not show that the companies or individuals concerned knowingly participated in every activity. Maxim Azarov, the owner of eServer, maintains that he has no direct commercial relationship with Stark Industries; that IP resources can move between providers; and that his company enforces strict rules against cybercrime.

items.descriptionTR:
In recent weeks, Ukrainian drones have targeted large warehouses across Russia, destroying millions of dollars of merchandise stored inside them.
These warehouses and logistics hubs belong to Wildberries, the Russian equivalent to Amazon.  Ukraine is taking aim at Ozon, Russia’s second-largest online retailer, too.
Ukraine says it’s targeting these companies because they’ve been providing supplies to soldiers on the front line.
But according to Matthew Sussex, associate professor in strategic studies at Deakin University in Australia, who talked to The Conversation Weekly podcast, Kyiv’s strategy also intends to disrupt the lives of everyday Russians.
When you put in an online order that can’t go through because the merchandise has been blown up by Ukrainian drones, that starts to put indirect political pressure on people like Vladimir Putin because it hits the everyday Russian consumer.
But as the war drags on well into its fourth year, is there anything that could put pressure on Putin to withdraw troops from Ukraine?
[Putin] has given no sign that he wants an off ramp. But the pressures that will build on him to seek one will continue to grow.
He really has staked his legacy on this invasion of Ukraine. And that’s something that would be really hard for him personally to back away from, in terms of his political longevity and his place in Russia’s history books.

Ukraine's drone operations are reportedly reaching consumer logistics and energy infrastructure beyond the front line in Russia. In the targeting of warehouse and logistics centres belonging to Wildberries and Ozon, it is argued that these companies supply materials to soldiers at the front; Matthew Sussex of Deakin University assesses that this may also be intended to create indirect political pressure on Vladimir Putin by disrupting everyday consumption.

Russian authorities reported that a refinery was hit in the Moscow region, homes were damaged and at least two people were killed. Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted since Saturday, 450 of them headed for Moscow. The extent of the damage at the refinery remains unclear.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that a major oil industry facility and logistics facilities had been hit; he said they were linked to the billions of dollars financing Russia's war machine. Repeated attacks on Russian refineries are also reported to have contributed to shortages of petroleum products and rising fuel prices.
slots.packetTitle: As war reaches into Russia's daily life

items.descriptionTR:
Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back
Sometimes, where I live in Kyiv, I hear people say: “This feels pre-war.” It refers to situations that remind us of what life was like before. You could call it a “sense of normalcy”.
For example, it refers to being able to walk around at night, travel abroad or plan your life at least six months in advance. Simple, everyday things have become a lost luxury.
items.titleTR: Meditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missiles | Anna Ivanenko

items.descriptionTR: The state post service delivers pensions, medicine and letters to people just miles from the front.
items.titleTR: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

slots.packetSpot:
Daily life under Russia's occupation continues both in the search for a brief sense of normality in Kyiv and in the postal service delivering pensions, medicine, food and communication to dangerous areas. Artist Anna Ivanenko describes signs of ordinariness such as going to the theatre, drinking coffee or making plans months ahead under the shadow of the threat of missiles and drones.

According to Igor Smelyansky, head of Ukrposhta, decisions must be made every day between the safety of teams and the needs of remote settlements. According to the institution, branches and vehicles have been targeted since 2022, and more than 50 employees have been killed. Postal workers such as Kateryna Marynych, who works near Zaporizhzhia, provide access to money, medicine and basic necessities despite the danger.
slots.packetTitle: Traces of daily life under occupation

items.descriptionTR: North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so, writes the BBC's Quentin Sommerville.
items.titleTR: Why a fresh wave of North Korean soldiers may fight in Russia's war in Ukraine

slots.packetSpot:
North Korean soldiers are expected to be deployed again and on a larger scale in Russia's war against Ukraine. North Korean workers are also reported to have been sent to the Yelabuga Drone Factory in the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan.

According to a Ukrainian intelligence estimate cited by the BBC, between 11,000 and 14,000 North Korean soldiers were initially deployed alongside Russian forces in the Kursk region; it is claimed that 3,000 were killed, 1,500 were wounded and around 8,500 remain on Russian territory. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that up to 50,000 additional North Korean soldiers could be sent to Russia.

According to Asia Times, the number of North Koreans working at the Geran drone production facility in Alabuga is increasing. The article cites estimates that between 12,000 and 25,000 of the facility's roughly 40,000 workers are North Korean; it stresses that assessments suggesting Russia could transfer drones or production technology to North Korea remain speculative for now.
