items.descriptionTR:
￼
Svetlana Evgrafova/Getty
As we reflect on 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks that killed almost 3,000 people, terrorism remains an ongoing yet evolving threat that defies easy answers.
“Once a terrorist, always a terrorist” is a familiar refrain. It reflects a common belief that all terrorist offenders are the same and rehabilitation programs simply don’t work.
A growing body of evidence tells a different story, suggesting some people genuinely can – and do – leave terrorism behind.
Our research looked at Australia’s longest-running program addressing the rehabilitation of those engaged in offending motivated by Salafi jihadism.
We found some participants don’t only stop offending, they also go on to build the skills and strengths to lead meaningful lives in line with their own values and interests.
No single path into or out of terrorism
The process that leads someone to get involved in terrorism is almost never down to just one cause or motivation. Instead, terrorist behaviour comes from a complex mix of factors, and how much each one matters differs from person to person.
Take ideology, for example, the set of political, religious or social beliefs a person or group uses to justify violence.
This plays a role in most people’s journeys into terrorism, but it cannot fully explain their behaviour or choices on its own. Ideology usually works together with other factors, especially relationships and the way a person’s social identity is formed.
For many people, becoming involved in terrorism is a way of meeting needs that aren’t being met elsewhere in their lives, such as a sense of belonging, purpose or significance.
Rebuilding a sense of identity
This matters a lot for how we think about people leaving terrorism behind. It means walking away from terrorist offending is far more complicated than simply quitting a group or a cause.
Successful disengagement is about finding something meaningful to engage with instead; something that lets a person thrive in a healthier, more social environment.
In other words, it’s not just about taking something away. It’s about building something new in its place.
One of the hardest parts of leaving terrorism behind seems to be rebuilding a sense of identity. Terrorist groups, including online extremist communities that support them, often give members a strong sense of belonging. When people leave, they frequently end up isolated and struggle to form new relationships or find purpose in their lives.
How well-designed programs can help
The Community Integration Support Program (CISP) was set up in Victoria in 2010, originally to help rehabilitate people whose offending was motivated by Salafi jihadism.
The program offers holistic, tailored support through a diverse team: religious mentors (community imams), case managers, clinical psychologists, an officer who helps participants move from prison back into the community, and a family support officer.
Our research gave us rare, in-depth access to key people involved, including 24 CISP participants, 20 of whom had been convicted of terrorism-related offences. Some were interviewed years into their rehabilitation.
We found reappraising their ideology helped the program participants move away from terrorism.
Disengagement often involves becoming more open-minded and willing to see nuance and grey areas, rather than seeing everything in black and white. This is usually built over years, through trusted relationships with mentors and unexpected acts of kindness from people once viewed as the enemy.
Several participants changed their beliefs genuinely through the process of being provided more knowledge, more contextual interpretation, more guidance, more care and respect, and more time. Over time, this let them feel safe enough to be vulnerable and to question the ideas and beliefs that had led to their crimes.
The religious mentors provided deeper knowledge, but it was the participants themselves who had to go through the difficult, sometimes humbling, process of reappraising what they believed.
Those who succeeded gained a lasting sense of humility and openness, something they could keep leaning on as they rebuilt their lives.
As one participant put it:
[The CISP taught me] to pay attention to context, that it’s not black and white […] It’s taught me humility. I was very judgemental before […] humbling was a difficult experience for me.
We also found that participants’ journeys into terrorism were often driven by moral considerations and values such as justice, compassion and self-sacrifice, but that those considerations were only extended to some and excluded others.
For these participants, leaving terrorism behind didn’t mean abandoning those values. It meant finding new, legitimate ways to express them, such as through service and a commitment to family, community, faith, and others they previously viewed as unworthy.
By redirecting these core values, participants found new sources of meaning and purpose after giving up their terrorist goals and the beliefs that went with them. This did not mean giving up their religion. Quite the opposite. It meant gaining a deeper and more nuanced understanding of their religious obligations.
A long journey
This is slow work. It takes real commitment from the imams and other staff, who accompany participants on a difficult but – for some – ultimately life-affirming journey, often over many years.
While a few participants show positive change quite quickly, most don’t start showing real, lasting change until three or more years into the program.
If we want fewer people to walk back into terrorism, the evidence suggests part of the answer is the patient, years-long work of helping them build a different life to walk toward instead.
￼
Ramon Spaaij receives funding from the Department of Home Affairs and Victoria Police.
Debra Smith receives funding from the Department of Home Affairs and Victoria Police.
Muhammad Iqbal receives funding from the Department of Home Affairs and Victoria Police.
Walking away from terrorist offending is far more complicated than simply quitting a group or a cause. But evidence shows well-designed programs can work.
items.titleTR: Can people truly walk away from terrorism? Inside the slow work of rehabilitation

items.descriptionTR: This 32-year-old from Montpellier, who grew up in a radicalized family and faces a possible life sentence, told the Paris special criminal court that he's discovered 'a new vision of life' since his imprisonment in France.
items.titleTR: The surprising deradicalization speech of jihadist Othman Garrido, on trial for beheadings in Syria

slots.packetSpot:
Research into the Community Integration Support Program, established in Victoria, Australia, in 2010, finds that people convicted of terrorism-related offences are offered religious mentors, case managers, clinical psychologists, support for the transition from prison to the community, and family support. Researchers say they observed, among some of the 24 participants examined, change towards not only moving away from crime but also developing a new sense of identity and purpose; lasting change often takes three years or longer.

According to the research, ideological reassessment, moving away from black-and-white thinking, and finding legitimate sources of meaning in areas such as family, community, faith or service can play a role in this process. The study does not claim that such changes occur in the same way for every participant or that the program alone produces outcomes.

At Paris's special criminal court, Othman Garrido, who is accused of taking part in beheadings in Syria, said that the six years he spent in French prisons, his reading of literature, his education and his vocational training changed his outlook. He also acknowledged that there would be those who doubted the sincerity of his testimony; it has not yet been established that this change occurred or that the allegations against him have been proven.

items.descriptionTR:
The Pentagon is considering big changes to how it positions US forces in Europe and the Middle East, in what could amount to a major military shake-up.
President Donald Trump's administration made it clear in this year's National Defence Strategy that it wants allies to do more in Europe and the Middle East so the US can focus on China and the Western Hemisphere, where Washington is increasingly targeting drug cartels in South America.
In the Gulf, the war in Iran has underscored how vulnerable troops posted to the region can be. At least 18 US service members have been killed, including six in an Iranian missile strike at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait.
"Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan," an inspector general's report into the costs of the war found.
￼
The report, released this week, also said Pentagon officials have yet to decide whether they will return base and troop levels to what they were before the war.
The Pentagon "has not determined what its future posture will be in the region, how it will construct its bases, and what percentage of the construction costs allies partners will contribute", the report states.
The Washington Post has reported that the Pentagon is looking at whether it will move troops away from the Gulf. Typically, about 40,000 US personnel are based across the region.
An official told the Post that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had not yet ordered a formal review of force posture in the Middle East.
CNN on Friday reported that the Pentagon is expected to send MQ-9 Reaper drones currently operating in Africa to be used in South America as the US increases its anti-narcotics operations.
Mr Hegseth in June announced a six-month review for Europe that is looking at the US troop presence there. The effort is led by Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of defence for policy, who has long advocated greater focus on deterring China.
Among the possibilities being considered by Pentagon officials, Reuters reported on Thursday, is withdrawing about 25,000 troops from Europe, a move that would worry European and Nato officials who are facing an increasingly confrontational Russia. The US currently has about 80,000 troops in Europe.
While reducing force levels in Europe or the Middle East could free up resources for other priorities, it also raises questions about US deterrence in both regions and the reliability of Washington's commitments.
Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the senior Democrat on the Senate foreign ⁠relations committee, on Thursday asked Secretary of State Marco Rubio to ensure that US diplomats are ⁠involved in the Pentagon-led review of America's military presence in Europe.
In a letter addressed to Mr Rubio, who is also National Security Adviser, Ms Shaheen said that diplomats, including US ambassadors, are being kept out of the loop.
"The Department of State, which is responsible for managing our bilateral relationships, has traditionally played a substantial role in reviews of this kind," she said in the letter.
"Yet what we are hearing through our own conversations, travel across Europe and engagement with our allies tells a different story. US ambassadors and chiefs of mission in affected countries have been excluded from consultations."
A State Department official disputed the issues raised in the letter, saying that diplomats were being consulted.
Ms Shaheen wrote that adjustments in troop levels ⁠would have an effect on bilateral relationships that the State Department would be left to manage, with the Baltic nations of Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia among the countries with the most at stake.
European leaders have warned of incidents, often attributed to Russia, that fall below the threshold of conventional military attacks but undermine European security – such as sabotage, arson and drone incursions.
items.titleTR: Pentagon considers changes to US 'force posture' in Middle East and Europe

slots.packetSpot:
Donald Trump said “major progress” had been made toward establishing a permanent U.S. Army base in Poland; the location of the base was not disclosed, and it has not been confirmed that it has been established. Poland already has about 10,000 rotational U.S. troops and 11 facilities; the U.S. Army Garrison is headquartered in Poznań. Trump had previously threatened to withdraw troops, then announced that 5,000 additional troops would be sent to Poland. The State Department also announced $4 billion in military aid for Poland in September.

The announcement comes as the Pentagon reassesses force deployments in Europe and the Middle East. According to Reuters, withdrawing as many as 25,000 of the roughly 80,000 U.S. troops in Europe is among the options; however, no decision has been made. While the Gulf normally has about 40,000 personnel, the Pentagon is also reported not yet to have reached a decision on future troop and base levels in the region.

The Europe review is being led by Elbridge Colby, the Defense Department's under secretary for policy. The administration aims to focus the United States on China and the Western Hemisphere while seeking greater responsibility from allies in Europe and the Middle East. CNN reported that MQ-9 Reaper drones operating in Africa could be shifted to South America, where counternarcotics activities are being stepped up.

At least 18 U.S. troops were reportedly killed during the Iran war, with six people killed in an Iranian missile attack on Port Shuaiba in Kuwait. An inspector general's report said hundreds of structures and facilities at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan were damaged or destroyed in Iranian attacks. Jeanne Shaheen, the senior Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, asked Secretary of State Marco Rubio to include diplomats in the Europe review; a State Department official disputed the claim that diplomats had been excluded. NATO allies, especially Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia, are concerned about possible changes in the face of Russia's increasingly confrontational stance.

items.descriptionTR: As the West continues to denounce Russian aggression in Ukraine and to support Kyiv with a host of economic and military measures, Russian President Vladimir Putin says that Nato is expanding its reach and influence with the intention of preparing for war with Russia. Analysis by Dr Alexander Titov, lecturer in Modern European History at Queen's University Belfast in the UK.
items.titleTR: Putin says Europe is 'preparing for war'

items.descriptionTR:
NATO's Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone's remarks follow multiple warnings by European leaders in recent days about a growing risk of Russian escalation.
NATO is ready to respond to a potential Russian escalation on Europe’s eastern flank, the alliance’s top general Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said Saturday, amid growing warnings of a possible staged attack by Moscow. 
“The alliance is ready, the structure is ready, the soldiers … the weapons are ready,” Dragone told reporters during a regular meeting of the alliance’s 32 top generals in Copenhagen, adding that NATO was continuing its work in “increasing” these forces “in number … and also in sophistication.”
The remarks follow growing warnings by European leaders about a possible Russian escalation in Europe. On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Moscow could send drones or missiles into a frontline NATO country in “the next few months” in a staged provocation to test the alliance — a risk that was later echoed by France and the Netherlands.
Europe has grappled with a growing number of airspace violations and sabotage attempts in recent weeks, as tensions with Russia continue to rise over its full-scale war in Ukraine. In August, U.S. intelligence reports warned that Moscow was planning a limited assault on a NATO country in the coming years.
Dragone, the chair of NATO’s military committee, said the alliance’s generals on Saturday did not discuss the latest warnings but argued NATO had “4,000 pages” of military plans ready for protecting its eastern flank, starting from scenarios involving a “minimal crisis or interference [on] our soil.” NATO allies agreed on three operational regional defense plans in 2023 following Moscow’s all-out invasion of Ukraine.
Allies are “ready in case of an escalation,” Dragone said. “In case of an attack, we know how to do it.” 
“Russia’s reckless behaviour over the last weeks and months … continues to test allied resolve” and “aims to undermine trust and weaken our unity,” Dragone said, adding: “I want to be clear — these attempts are not dividing us. They are sharpening our tools, making us much more united and determined.”
items.titleTR: NATO ‘ready’ for potential Russian false flag attack, alliance’s top general says

slots.packetSpot:
Vladimir Putin portrays NATO's expansion of its reach and influence as preparation for war with Russia. Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of NATO's Military Committee, said the alliance was ready for a possible Russian escalation or staged provocation on Europe's eastern flank.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Moscow could embark on a provocation in the coming months that might test the alliance by sending a drone or missile into a NATO country on the front line; France and the Netherlands voiced similar concerns. While airspace violations and attempted sabotage were reported, US intelligence assessments also contained warnings that Moscow could plan a limited attack on a NATO country in the coming years.

Dragone stated that NATO had military plans to protect its eastern flank and that the alliance knew how it would act in the event of an attack. NATO allies had agreed on three regional defence plans in 2023 following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

items.descriptionTR: ￼ The Iran war has cost the United States at least $45.1 billion, military officials said. The amount covers the conflict through early September.
items.titleTR: Iran war has cost Pentagon at least $45.1 billion

slots.packetSpot:
The publicly disclosed human and financial toll of the US war against Iran is a matter of debate. According to information Pentagon officials provided to Congress, the cost of the war had reached at least $45.1 billion by early September; that figure does not include the cost of repairing damage at overseas bases and facilities. The Congressional Budget Office, meanwhile, estimated the cost at about $38 billion as of 1 August. Official projections indicate that the Department of Defense may spend $2 billion to $3 billion a month from now on.

Meanwhile, it was reported that the Pentagon's public Defense Casualty Analysis System does not include the deaths of two US service members. Major Sorffly Davius, serving with the 42nd Infantry Division at Camp Buehring in Kuwait, was announced to have died on 6 March of undetermined causes; Sergeant Devin Seibel was announced to have died on 31 May in a training-related incident at Erbil Air Base. Seibel's death is under investigation.

While the record system shows 18 deaths, information attributed to unnamed US officials in the report refers to at least 22, while another official's statement refers to 23 military deaths; it was also stated that three contractors in the US Central Command area have died since the start of the conflict. These figures do not form a single definitive total. Democrats in Congress are demanding a more detailed and transparent accounting of the casualties and spending. The Pentagon, meanwhile, criticized reports concerning the deaths.

items.descriptionTR: Young South Africans are not apathetic but increasingly unconvinced that voting translates into accountability, as broken promises and unresponsive local institutions erode trust in democracy. The answer is not another lecture to ‘show up’, but a system that keeps a visible ledger of promises, performance and consequences.

items.descriptionTR: Decaying municipalities, dry taps and raw sewage are now matched by public representatives’ open insolence, proving that political failure in South Africa is matched by profound contempt.
items.titleTR: Foot in mouth — politicians talk sh#t while South Africans live in it

slots.packetSpot:
The temporary closure imposed after the bodies of at least nine women were found in Ekurhuleni has brought the public safety debate to the fore alongside failures in municipal services and policing. Political actors argue that non-functioning streetlights, a lack of cameras, long grass and around 300 metro police vehicles waiting in workshops create conditions conducive to crime. Allegations concerning crime within the police, corruption and accountability problems are also on the agenda at the Madlanga Commission; Julius Mkhwanazi faces charges in separate cases.

One commentary on young voters argues that the belief that the ballot box does not produce accountable outcomes is growing stronger. Another commentary describes dry taps and sewage flowing in the open as signs of decay in municipal governance. In these assessments, the failure of local institutions emerges as an issue that erodes not only daily life but also democratic trust.

items.descriptionTR:
The industry is the top donor in the midterm elections, with tens of millions for various candidates in the expectation Trump will maintain his support for the sector
In July 2024, during a crypto conference held in Nashville, Donald Trump vowed that if he returned to the White House he would turn the U.S. into the crypto capital of the world. Two years later, the largest market for digital assets still lacks a law to regulate the industry, while Europe has had one since December 2024. On Tuesday, the Senate blocked the progress of the Clarity Act yet again, citing insufficient safeguards to prevent public officials — including the president himself — from benefiting from their crypto businesses. Despite the legislative setback for a bill that includes many of the industry’s proposals, the sector has not lost faith: crypto firms and entrepreneurs continue to pour money into Republicans and pro-crypto candidates ahead of the November midterm elections.

items.descriptionTR: President Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., poured an additional $5 million into the Texas Senate race, according to a new Federal Election Commission (FEC) filing published Saturday.  The funds were earmarked for Del Ray Media LLC, a Virginia-based political media company, for TV and digital advertising against the Democratic nominee in this race, state Rep.…
items.titleTR: Trump’s MAGA Inc. funnels another $5 million into Texas Senate race

slots.packetSpot:
As the 2026 midterm elections approach, outside political spending aligned with Republicans is accelerating. According to Federal Election Commission records, Trump-linked MAGA Inc. had about $403 million in cash as of the end of July; over the past two weeks, three Trump-linked super PACs have booked more than $136.5 million in advertising in House and Senate races.

The Senate race in Texas is one focus of this activity. MAGA Inc. reportedly transferred another $5 million to Del Ray Media LLC for television and digital advertisements against James Talarico; the same entity had previously provided $10 million for two attack ads. MAGA Inc. is reported to have committed about $10 million for Texas, while Elon Musk-backed America PAC is said to have added about $2.6 million. In records from the end of June, Talarico had about $21.5 million on hand, compared with about $1.8 million for his Republican rival Ken Paxton; Paxton’s campaign also received about $54 million from the Texas arm of the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund. The race is considered competitive.

The crypto sector is also maintaining its presence in election financing despite the Clarity Act’s failure to advance in a procedural Senate vote. Advancing the bill, which includes regulation of digital assets, the division of oversight between the SEC and CFTC, and investor protections, fell short of the required 60 votes, with 49 votes in favor and 50 against. According to Public Citizen’s analysis based on OpenSecrets and Federal Election Commission data, the sector has spent a total of $206 million on candidates and PACs from both parties during the current election cycle; the most prominent support is directed toward Republican and crypto-friendly candidates.

items.descriptionTR:
Instead, constrain it legally and fight it politically. The world is watching
Far-right nationalist populist parties are making the running everywhere from Washington to Warsaw. So why be so alarmed about a little regional electoral victory for one such party, the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), in one federal state, Saxony-Anhalt? “Because it’s Germany!” is the almost instinctive answer in many heads around the world.
But that “because it’s Germany” needs to be taken apart, like the segments of an orange. Yes, because of Adolf Hitler, two dictatorships (Nazi Germany until 1945, communist-ruled East Germany until 1989) and two world wars. And yes, some of the language used by the AfD will give anyone familiar with Nazi rhetoric a cold shudder down the spine.
Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book, Europe in 7 1/2 Chapters, is published in October

Germany’s CDU is entering a leadership crisisDiego Faßnacht reports that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is facing a deepening leadership crisis as the CDU’s firewall strategy against the AfD breaks down. With no obvious successor ready
items.titleTR: Merz faces a leadership challenge without a challenger

slots.packetSpot:
The debate over what line to pursue against the AfD in Germany ranges from calls for a ban to legal constraints and political struggle. Timothy Garton Ash argues that the party should neither be banned nor incorporated into the normal political process; instead, it should be legally constrained and politically defeated.

According to Ash, if it becomes likely that the AfD will form a state government in Saxony-Anhalt, federal authorities should, where necessary, use their powers, including Article 37, which permits them to invalidate states’ actions that run counter to the constitutional order. He says this approach could involve preventing sensitive intelligence on Russia’s growing aggression from being shared with a state domestic security agency controlled by the AfD; protecting the independence of courts and prosecutors, and the neutrality of the police and civil service.

There are also those within the CDU who argue that the political “firewall” separating it from the AfD should be removed and that the party should be worked with. Ash writes that findings compiled by political scientists show that such a strategy of inclusion may also strengthen nationalists. Diego Faßnacht reports that, with the CDU’s firewall strategy unraveling, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is facing a deepening leadership crisis; no clear figure has emerged who could replace him.
slots.packetTitle: Germany's narrowing ground against the AfD

items.descriptionTR:
More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias Afwerki
More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.
Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.
items.titleTR: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers

items.descriptionTR: The children of key politicians jailed 25 years ago without a trace in Eritrea want answers.
items.titleTR: 'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago

slots.packetSpot:
Relatives of two separate groups whose fate has remained uncertain since the wave of press and political repression in Eritrea in 2001 are still seeking answers. A letter led by PEN International calls for verified proof of life for 12 writers and critics held without contact with the outside world, while the children of politicians in the G-15 say they do not know whether their parents are alive.

According to the BBC, G-15 members were detained in September 2001 after writing an open letter to President Isaias Afwerki calling for the implementation of the approved constitution and national elections. It is stated that nothing has been heard from Petros Solomon, Aster Yohannes, Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo and Aster Fissehatsion since their detention. Political prisoners are believed to be held in prisons including Ela-Ero and Karshelli; however, there has been no official statement on where these individuals are or whether they are alive.

It is reported that no national elections have been held in Eritrea since independence in 1993, and that Afwerki has remained in power.

slots.packetSpot:
Julia Loktev’s documentary follows the lives in exile of around a dozen journalists, most of them women, who left Russia during a period of mounting pressure on independent media. The film recounts how the journalists, while continuing their opposition to the Putin government, face new difficulties in delivering news to Russian-speaking citizens.

In the United States, Donald Trump reportedly barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists from entering the White House, and their press passes were also reportedly taken away. The White House Correspondents’ Association and various media outlets described the move as an intervention against press freedom and as unconstitutional; Trump did not give a specific reason for the ban.

In Guinea, the High Authority of Communication banned France 24 from broadcasting and withdrew the accreditations of the channel’s staff in the country. The same body also revoked the accreditation of Diawo Barry, a Jeune Afrique correspondent; the Committee to Protect Journalists called for the decisions to be reversed.

Two bail decisions in South Asia led to different outcomes. In Delhi, a court granted bail to Scottish national Jagtar Singh Johal, who was detained in 2017 in Punjab on charges alleged to be linked to terrorism. However, Johal remained in custody because the bail conditions and bond amounts have not yet been clarified.

In Pakistan, human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband were reportedly detained again hours after the country’s highest court suspended their sentences in a cybercrime case and granted them bail, their lawyers said.

items.titleTR: Bolivia slashes diesel subsidies as its Congress ratifies $1.9 billion IMF deal to ease deep economic crisis

items.descriptionTR: French fishermen renewed protests over rising fuel costs on Thursday despite the government increasing subsidies for the sector and extending support for farmers and construction companies. Diesel prices are nearing a record high, fuelling wider concern over the cost of living and calls for protests reminiscent of the Yellow Vest movement, seven months before the presidential election.
items.titleTR: French fishermen renew protest as France boosts aid over soaring fuel prices

items.descriptionTR:
Germany issues its relief measures as its finance minister calls on Brussels to draft a windfall tax proposal on oil companies.
Germany will lower tax on petrol and diesel by 17 cents per liter in a relief package worth €2.5 billion, the German government announced Friday.
“Those who rely on their cars every day are reaching their financial limits. … The relief package of €2.5 billion is no small sum in times of strained budgets,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said. The tax discount is to be implemented next month.
The measure, brokered between Germany’s federal and state governments, is part of the package promised by Merz as fuel prices continue to climb in response to the war in Iran and the escalating conflict between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
Two weeks ago, a key oil benchmark reached $100 a barrel for the first time since July following the latest escalations in the Middle East, sending pump prices soaring all over Europe.
The Merz government also plans to introduce a temporary fuel price cap on petrol and diesel modeled on similar policies in Luxembourg and Belgium. The price cap would take into account price moves on the oil markets, transportation and distribution costs, and retailers’ profit margins. Berlin aims to introduce the measure by Jan. 1, 2027.  Germany, through the voice of its Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, is among the EU member countries calling for a bloc-wide windfall tax on oil companies that have reaped billions of euros in excess profits since the start of the war. The topic is high on the agenda at an informal meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday and Saturday.  Ahead of the meeting on Friday, Klingbeil has called on the European Commission to present a proposal by the end of October.  “Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil, from Germany’s Social Democratic Party, told reporters. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”  But Merz’s conservatives have pushed back on the proposal. Germany’s Economic Affairs and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche said a windfall tax would only make sense in case of abusive price increases, she told Handelsblatt.  “The fact that eleven refineries are producing in Germany makes us less dependent on foreign countries; that must not be put at risk,” Reiche said.
items.titleTR: Germany cuts fuel tax as Middle East conflicts send prices soaring

items.descriptionTR:
Syria has announced it will offer subsidised diesel for heating, agriculture and industry, days after demonstrations erupted across the country over a fuel price rise.
The decision has raised questions among experts about the effectiveness and durability of the measure, as broader social grievances continue to brew.
"People are frustrated and are waiting for realistic solutions to their problems in general," said one protester, Ayman Asfara from Idlib. "If they do not see results from the first protests, there will be further protests, but this time with greater awareness."
Energy Minister Mohammed Al Bashir said that the government recognised that higher energy prices “have a direct impact on people’s livelihoods and on the agricultural, production and service sectors”.
“Our responsibility is not limited to securing petroleum products. It also includes seeking solutions that ease the burden, while maintaining continuity of supply,” he added.
Benjamin Feve, a senior consultant at Karam Shaar Advisory, said the move could have harmful consequences for the economy and lead to a waste of Syria's already scarce public funds.
“Fuel subsidies distort prices across the economy, encourage overconsumption and create incentives for smuggling,” he said. “They are also regressive because the people who consume the most fuel benefit the most.”
Mr Al Bashir said subsidised diesel would be sold at 115 Syrian pounds ($0.94) per litre for heating, agriculture and consumers eligible for government support. A second grade would be sold at 150 pounds per litre for some production and service sectors.
The standard grade would remain at 175 pounds per litre, while petrol and gas prices would not change. The standard diesel price remains below its actual cost of 206 pounds per litre, Mr Al Bashir told a media conference in Damascus, where he was joined by Syrian Petroleum Company chief executive Yousef Qablawi.
Mr Al Bashir also said several small local refineries would resume operations under the management and supervision of the Syrian Petroleum Company, bringing their combined crude oil processing capacity to about 35,000 barrels per day. SPC chief, Mr Qablawi, said the company had begun drawing up an implementation plan for the measures after discussions with the ministry.
It remains unclear how long the subsidy will stay in place and how much it will cost the government. “Nobody can really answer where the money will come from except the government,” Mr Feve told The National.
Despite the lifting of western sanctions, Syria is still reeling from decades of economic isolation and years of war, which have left the country facing a reconstruction bill of hundreds of billions of dollars. “The budget is already deeply in deficit, by more than $1 billion. This was precisely one of the reasons subsidies were lifted in the first place,” he added.
The subsidies could be funded by allied countries, but this would risk making Syria dependent on foreign support and political agendas. “At the end of the day, it would be a donation, not a sustainable policy for the Syrian government,” he said.
Widespread protests
The decision to cut diesel prices came after a meeting with President Ahmad Al Shara on Wednesday night to discuss the fuel crisis that has led to protests, in a major test for the government that replaced the Assad regime.
The Ministry of Energy raised fuel prices by between 25 and 40 per cent last Saturday. The price rise came against the backdrop of the phasing out of what remained of the Assad government’s subsidy system, as the Syria's new authorities have pledged a shift towards a free-market economy.
The ministry said the increase in the cost of petroleum products reflected rising global oil prices and coincided with the temporary shutdown of the Baniyas refinery for a major overhaul, which has increased Syria’s dependence on more expensive fuel imports, Mr Al Bashir said. Global energy prices have increased sharply since the outbreak of the Iran war in February.
The move sparked some of the most widespread protests since the fall of the Assad regime, particularly in eastern and northern Syria, with demonstrators demanding that the increase be reversed.
Syrians rely heavily on diesel to run generators amid widespread power cuts. The fuel is also crucial for transport, adding further strain on a population already struggling with economic hardship after decades of western sanctions. About 90 per cent of Syrians live below the poverty line, UN estimates show.
Protesters have also questioned how Syria’s highly publicised economic reopening has seemingly benefited only a fortunate few, who have been displaying wealth rarely seen before, while doing little to ease the hardship faced by struggling households.
“Fuel prices went up, while at the same time people could see with their own eyes delegations coming and going, cars being replaced, new cars in the hands of a certain group of people,” Mr Asfara from Idlib, who took part in the protests, told The National. “At the same time, Syrians don’t have enough to eat, drink or to afford medical care.”
He said the fuel protests were just one symptom of a growing divide between social classes, meaning people were either very poor or very wealthy. There has also been a "complete absence" of support for the reconstruction and repair of homes, he said.
“People didn’t take to the streets just because of fuel. It was similar during the revolution: people weren’t protesting only because of what happened to the children of Deraa.”
Fuel was the trigger, Mr Feve said, but it may not have been the main cause. “Grievances have been accumulating, particularly in rural areas and outside the main cities.”
The difference, he added, is the breadth of the protests, which have spread beyond sectors. “Fuel touches everyone. It affects transport, generators, the price of bread, the cost of getting to work and heating your home.”
“It is one price that turns a series of separate complaints into a single shared grievance,” he said.
items.titleTR: ‘People can’t take it any more’: Syrian government cuts diesel prices after protests over fuel costs

items.descriptionTR: [Daily News] Zanzibar -- FUEL and fertiliser subsidies, tax relief on essential food imports and tighter market price monitoring are among measures being used to curb inflation and protect the purchasing power of the currency, the House of Representatives heard yesterday.
items.titleTR: Tanzania: Fuel, Fertiliser Subsidies to Ease Inflation

slots.packetSpot:
As fuel costs rise, governments are not moving in the same direction. In Bolivia, after Congress approved a $1.9 billion IMF loan agreement, President Rodrigo Paz announced that diesel subsidies would be removed immediately, while support for petrol would continue for the time being. The IMF executive board must approve the programme before its funds are released. Paz also announced around $79 million in cash support for approximately 2.9 million people and concessional loans for groups affected by higher diesel costs.

In France, as rising diesel prices pushed fishers back into protest, the government raised support for the sector from 25 cents to 35 cents per litre; it also extended until the end of the year support for eligible construction and public works companies and farmers. Germany, meanwhile, announced a €2.5 billion package including a 17-cent-per-litre tax cut on petrol and diesel; it plans to introduce a temporary price cap from January 2027. Berlin also supports an EU-wide windfall tax on oil companies; Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche said this would be meaningful only in cases of abusive price increases.

In Syria, following fuel price rises of between 25% and 40% and protests, subsidised diesel at 115 Syrian pounds per litre was announced for heating, agriculture and consumers eligible for support. The price of standard diesel remained at 175 pounds, while petrol and gas prices were unchanged. The temporary closure of the Baniyas refinery for maintenance had increased dependence on more expensive fuel imports; the government reported that some small refineries would resume operations. In Zanzibar, it was also announced that fuel and fertiliser subsidies, tax cuts on staple food imports, market oversight, monetary policy and measures aimed at increasing food production were being used to contain inflation.

These choices make two distinct approaches visible in response to the pressure of fuel prices on household budgets and production costs: on one side, those expanding support to reduce the financial burden; on the other, those withdrawing subsidies amid fiscal crisis and external financing conditions. In Syria, however, uncertainty remains over how long the support will continue and how it will be funded.

items.descriptionTR: A $1tn sales pitch, more than 160 projects on offer, pivot to the EU amid a bitter trade war with the US - takeaways from the first Canada Investment Summit.
items.titleTR: Five takeaways from Canada's push to woo the world's richest investors

items.descriptionTR: Shipping on the Great Lakes has depended on a U.S. economy that moved in lockstep with Canada. A trade war is upending that balance.
items.titleTR: Great Lakes that bind U.S.-Canada trade are imperiled by Trump tariffs

slots.packetSpot:
As the trade dispute with the United States continues, Canada presented itself to major investors at the Toronto summit as a “safe haven” amid geopolitical and economic uncertainty. Mark Carney said that more than 160 projects had been presented to over 100 major investors; that his government was working on tax incentives, faster permitting processes for major projects and a one-year review target. The prime minister had pledged to attract C$1 trillion in investment over five years; the Prime Minister’s Office said the summit had generated interest in roughly C$500 billion in new investment.

Carney’s proposal to open the operation of four major airports to private investment envisages the federal government retaining ownership of the land and core assets. Lily Chang of the Canadian Labour Congress argued that the move would be detrimental to workers and passengers, while Nick Barry-Shaw of the Council of Canadians described the summit as privatization.

Canada and the United States have been imposing reciprocal tariffs since trade talks abruptly collapsed last month. While some of the new US tariffs have taken effect, others have been lifted; bans targeting products such as alcohol and motorcycles are also expected to come into force the following week. Carney is preparing to travel to Europe to discuss a distinctive alliance with the European Union in the fields of security and the economy; Canada’s close ties with the United States nevertheless continue.

The tariffs are also straining the transportation balance in the Great Lakes, where the two countries’ economies have long operated in an intertwined way. The trade war simultaneously makes visible the direct pressure on cross-border trade and Canada’s search to deepen its economic partnerships with Europe, Asia and the Middle East.
slots.packetTitle: Canada seeks its bearings under pressure from the south

items.descriptionTR: Massad Boulos, senior adviser to the US president on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs, said Donald Trump was working to end the months-long war, pointing out he was a "person who delivers".
items.titleTR: Trump determined to end Iran war soon, US president's senior adviser tells Euronews

items.descriptionTR:
The US is working with regional and international partners on a diplomatic push to secure a humanitarian truce in Sudan, which has been engulfed in a three-year civil war, a senior White House adviser has said.
US President Donald Trump's adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, spoke to Sky News Arabia about Washington's efforts with fellow Quad countries – the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Egypt – as well as Turkey, Qatar and European nations to establish a new path towards a ceasefire.
"Today we are striving, together with our brothers in the Quad, namely Egypt, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as our brothers in Qatar and Turkey and in Europe, towards a new peaceful path," he said in an interview broadcast on Saturday.
Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has devastated the country of 50 million people and battered its economy. International efforts aimed at ending the war have struggled to secure a lasting cessation of hostilities.
Asked whether the US could force open humanitarian corridors, Mr Boulos said Washington was working with international and regional partners on the issue. He said the goal remained to secure a humanitarian truce as the first step towards a wider political settlement.
Mr Boulos said the US continued to support the "comprehensive peace plan” he announced in February. The plan is centred on five pillars – an immediate humanitarian truce; sustained humanitarian access and civilian protection; a permanent ceasefire; a political transition to a civilian-led government; and postwar reconstruction.
￼
"There is no military solution in Sudan," he said. "The only solution is a peaceful solution."
A UN fact-finding report revealed this month that the SAF used foreign-supplied drones in operations that harmed civilians. While the reported repeated that external players had supported the RSF by enabling the transfer of weapons, it cast a harsher light on the SAF's actions.
Arms embargo push
As part of its efforts to end the war, the US has also been working to expand an existing UN arms embargo in Darfur to cover the entire country, especially over the use of drones, which Mr Boulos described as a defining feature of the war. "It is fundamentally a war of drones," he said.
The UN Security Council this month gave members one month to discuss the US proposal. Washington pushed for that short-term extension to allow further negotiations to widen the embargo, rather than simply renewing the existing sanctions regime for another year.
Mr Boulos said Washington did not view the move as a failure and would use the additional time to negotiate with members of the Security Council, including Russia and China, which had opposed the expansion of the measures.
He said the US and its partners wanted to end foreign military support for both sides in Sudan. Washington has also imposed sanctions on people, groups and foreign companies accused of supporting either side. Mr Boulos said other measures in addition to the arms embargo included action against the illicit gold trade and use of chemical weapons.
He said the administration of President Donald Trump, as well as the previous administration, had reached the conclusion that chemical weapons were used in Sudan. The issue, he said, must now be addressed through the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons rather than directly by Washington.
The US has offered technical assistance to help resolve the issue, he said, adding that the SAF "must address this matter with the [OPCW]."
This month, the SAF faced new evidence over its use of chemical weapons. Reports published by The New York Times, The Washington Post and Euronews revealed the SAF had not only used chemical weapons in the devastating war but also built a stockpile that it has since sought to conceal. A dossier provided details of how the SAF tested bombs in Sudan’s desert and built up its chemical weapons operation piece by piece, before attempting to cover its tracks.
Both sides have been accused of war crimes and the US has increased pressure on the country's warring commanders – SAF leader Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan and RSF chief Gen Mohamed Dagalo – maintaining that neither can have a role in governing the country after the war. While the RSF has said it accepts a 90-day humanitarian truce, it has rejected aspects of the proposed withdrawal arrangements. Gen Al Burhan, meanwhile, has vowed to continue fighting until the RSF is defeated.
Civilian-led peace
Mr Boulos said the opposition to both sides was part of the roadmap agreed to by the Quad and that it was up to the Sudanese people to decide on their post-war government. He stressed that the US does not formally recognise the SAF-backed government but has dealt with it as a de facto entity.
"At the same time, we do not recognise any parallel governments and we oppose partition," he said, adding that the US supports a unified Sudan and warned against a "repeat of the Libyan scenario in Sudan". Libya has also been divided by civil war, with two rival governments in place.
Dialogue for a political solution must be inclusive, but concerns remain over the Muslim Brotherhood and extremist groups that should be excluded from the process, he said.
"Apart from that, there must be very broad national participation," he said. Sudan's diverse civil society groups, political parties and other entities need to be included, he added.
items.titleTR: US working with partners on push for humanitarian truce in Sudan, says Trump adviser

items.descriptionTR: World leaders head to the UN General Assembly as Gulf states seek renewed diplomacy to reduce attacks, restore more predictable energy flows and move the Iran war away from active conflict. Suzanne Maloney of the Brookings Institution joins David Gura and Christina Ruffini on Bloomberg This Weekend and says disruptions to Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline and other regional infrastructure are adding urgency to those efforts as Gulf economies face mounting pressure from the conflict. (Source: Bloomberg)
items.titleTR: UN Talks Offer a New Opening on Iran War

slots.packetSpot:
As the war in Iran and the civil war in Sudan continue, external actors are trying to ease the conflicts through negotiations, a humanitarian ceasefire and United Nations diplomacy. Donald Trump’s senior adviser Massad Boulos said Trump believes the Iran war will end soon and is determined to end it; however, he gave no timetable. According to Boulos, negotiations are being given an opportunity, and the nuclear issue needs to be resolved for the war to stop.

Gulf countries, meanwhile, want diplomacy at the UN to be revived in order to move the Iran war out of active conflict, reduce attacks and make energy flows more predictable. Disruptions to Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline and other infrastructure in the region are said to be increasing pressure on Gulf economies.

In Sudan, the US is seeking a humanitarian ceasefire with the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye and European countries. Washington’s plan includes an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, as well as humanitarian access and the protection of civilians, a permanent ceasefire, a civilian-led political transition and post-war reconstruction. While Boulos argues that there is no military solution in Sudan, it is reported that the Rapid Support Forces accepted a 90-day humanitarian ceasefire but rejected some elements of withdrawal arrangements; Abdel Fattah Al Burhan, meanwhile, is reported to have said he would continue fighting until the Rapid Support Forces are defeated.

Boulos stated that the US is seeking to extend the UN arms embargo in Darfur to all of Sudan, and that Russia and China oppose the expansion. While the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces face accusations of war crimes, it is stated that US allegations that the Sudanese Armed Forces used chemical weapons, and findings indicated by published investigations, should be addressed through the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons.
slots.packetTitle: Diplomacy in the shadow of war

items.titleTR: South Korean president urges Trump dialogue with Pyongyang

items.descriptionTR: Pyongyang's willingness to accept aid remains unclear as inter-Korean exchanges and dialogue channels are virtually non-existent
items.titleTR: South Korea plans to deliver over 1,400 medical items to North Korea as humanitarian assistance

slots.packetSpot:
Seoul is seeking two separate paths to re-engage with Pyongyang. President Lee Jae Myung said he had encouraged Donald Trump to continue dialogue with North Korea and that they were conducting advance coordination to facilitate US-North Korea talks. According to Lee, such a meeting would be difficult, but not impossible.

Trump said in August that he wanted to meet Kim Jong-un within the year, but gave no details. While North Korea gave a limited response to those remarks, Kim Yo Jong described the latest US-led drills as a “war rehearsal” and said the policy of strengthening nuclear deterrence would not change.

Seoul is also planning to send 1,431 items of equipment to a hospital in Pyongyang under a humanitarian medical support programme. The estimated value of the materials in 166 categories is $6.75 million. Implementation of the plan depends on talks with North Korea; whether Pyongyang will accept the aid is also uncertain. South Korea had obtained an exemption from the UN sanctions committee for the equipment in May. While some lawmakers voiced concern that the materials could be used for other purposes, Unification Minister Chung Dong-young argued that humanitarian aid should not be tied to North Korea’s military policy.
slots.packetTitle: Seoul reaches Pyongyang by two routes

items.titleTR: Iran expels Swedish diplomat in tit-for-tat after Stockholm's move

items.descriptionTR: Bosnia's expulsion of two Serbian embassy staff, in response to the honours given to Ratko Mladic's funeral, draws angry response from Serbia and Bosnian Serb officials – who questioned its legitimacy. Bosnia's expulsion of two Serbian embassy staff, in response to the honours given to Ratko Mladic's funeral, draws angry response from Serbia and Bosnian Serb officials – who questioned its legitimacy.
items.titleTR: Serbia, Bosnian Serbs Slate Sarajevo’s Expulsion of Diplomats over Mladic

slots.packetSpot:
The reciprocal expulsions between Tehran and Stockholm came after mutual accusations concerning the activities of diplomatic missions. Sweden expelled a diplomat serving at the Iranian embassy in Stockholm over activities it said were incompatible with the Vienna Convention; it gave no details. Iran, too, gave a Swedish diplomat 48 hours to leave the country and described Stockholm's decision as unfounded.

In Sarajevo, meanwhile, Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic announced that he had declared military attaché Milan Dulanovic and BIA adviser Danko Maksimovic from the Serbian embassy persona non grata, after Serbia held a military funeral ceremony in Belgrade for convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić. The two personnel were reportedly given 48 hours.

While Serbia and officials in the Serb-majority Republika Srpska entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina condemned the move, the Serb member of Bosnia and Herzegovina's tripartite presidency also joined the dispute over authority. Under a 2004 regulation, the authority to expel heads of diplomatic missions rests with the presidency; in certain cases, the foreign minister has authority over other embassy personnel. According to the Serb member, one of the two personnel had already completed his assignment and left Bosnia and Herzegovina.

items.descriptionTR:
Beijing believes slowdown calls aim to lock in US advantage, and is pursuing a different balance between safety and pace
About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
items.titleTR: Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development

items.descriptionTR:
At the start of this week, the who's-who of AI seemed - at least tentatively - on the side of AI regulation. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had proposed a three-step plan for slowing AI development, including by embedding third-party evaluators in labs, coordinating across the domestic industry, and forging international agreements potentially […]
￼

At the start of this week, the who's-who of AI seemed - at least tentatively - on the side of AI regulation. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had proposed a three-step plan for slowing AI development, including by embedding third-party evaluators in labs, coordinating across the domestic industry, and forging international agreements potentially with government assistance. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk publicly seemed to agree on aspects of all three things.
Anthropic and OpenAI had already been dropping hints that they and other labs were working on some kind of …
items.titleTR: The AI regulation smackdown isn’t over

slots.packetSpot:
In the debate over how quickly advanced artificial intelligence should progress, China sees US-backed calls for a slowdown as an attempt to limit its own technological advancement. Beijing’s approach is based on encouraging the spread of AI while setting safety boundaries through the state; the updated framework also covers agents, cybersecurity threats that advanced models could give rise to, and the possibility of AI improving itself.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, meanwhile, advocates setting a global pace for advanced AI. His proposal envisages third-party evaluations in laboratories, coordination within the industry and international regulations that could also require cooperation with China; he also supports maintaining export controls on advanced chips and machines.

This line is not a shared position within US AI circles either. While Sam Altman of OpenAI, Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind and Elon Musk of SpaceX appear to agree with some elements of the proposal, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said companies themselves should determine the pace needed to train their models safely. Trump described concerns that AI could destroy humanity as a “hoax.”

items.descriptionTR:
￼
The camera on a robot vacuum cleaner captured this cat. What else did it capture around the house? voorts/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA
A husband in Taiwan suspected his wife of having an affair. In September 2023, he found a used toothbrush at their holiday home, and garage video showed an unfamiliar man driving his wife there. Three months later, he opened their robot vacuum’s app to speak with her and saw an intimate encounter through its live camera.
He recorded the feed and used it to win about US$16,000 from his wife and her lover for infringing on his marital rights. Then the Taoyuan District Court sentenced him to five months in jail and fined him roughly $4,700 for recording private activity without consent.
Both rulings are defensible. Together, they expose a troubling gap: Devices in homes now generate evidence continuously and often invisibly, while the governing law remains a patchwork. As faculty members in a school of interdisciplinary forensics, we see such cases where forensic practice meets law that has not kept pace.
The house that watches
A modern robot vacuum is a mobile sensor platform. Some models combine cameras, microphones, laser navigation and remote video access, while app-connected models create detailed floor maps and cleaning histories. Their data may also reach manufacturers’ servers.
In 2022, MIT Technology Review revealed images from development versions of iRobot’s Roomba J7, including a woman on a toilet. Test-household images had gone to a data-labeling contractor, where workers posted them in private social media groups. No hacking was required; the leak arose from the ordinary pipeline used to train object-recognition software.
Digital witnesses are already testifying
Courts have confronted household data for years. Arkansas prosecutors charged James Bates with murder after a friend died in his hot tub, then sought recordings from his Amazon Echo and cited smart-meter data suggesting overnight water use. Amazon resisted until Bates consented. However, prosecutors could not eliminate other reasonable explanations, and they eventually dropped the charge.
In Connecticut, Richard Dabate claimed that an intruder murdered his wife, Connie. Her Fitbit data contradicted his timeline and helped establish when she stopped moving. A jury convicted him, and in 2025, the Connecticut Supreme Court upheld the conviction and found the Fitbit evidence scientifically reliable.
In Ohio, Ross Compton’s pacemaker data was used to challenge his account of a house fire, raising a novel Fourth Amendment question: How much privacy protection should apply to intimate medical data generated by an implanted device? The court ultimately upheld the search warrant, finding probable cause and concluded that obtaining the data remotely was not an unreasonable search. Compton died before his arson trial date.
In short, household data can convict, exonerate or mislead. That makes digital forensics indispensable and demands careful guardrails.
￼
The gray dimple on top of this Roomba robot vacuum cleaner contains a camera. Kārlis Dambrāns/Flickr, CC BY-NC
Three problems the law has not solved
First is consent and notice. The wife in Taiwan argued that small indicator lights gave no meaningful warning, a concern that extends to guests, children, domestic workers and estranged spouses. Unlike a mounted security camera, a roaming appliance may record people who never saw its privacy policy.
Second, legality and admissibility do not always align. The constitutional exclusionary rule restrains government, not private parties, so the Fourth Amendment generally does not bar evidence wrongfully obtained by a private actor. The Supreme Court established that principle in Burdeau v. McDowellin 1921.
How do the courts admit evidence potentially generated and extracted by private individuals? In the Taiwan case, what exactly was recorded? Where was it stored? Was it altered? These questions go beyond whether the video appears authentic; they determine what a court can reliably infer from a digital artifact whose chain of custody may begin with a participant in the dispute.
Congress created a different rule for aural communications. Under the federal Wiretap Act of 1968, illegally intercepted wire or oral communications may be excluded, and the interceptor may face criminal and civil liability. When the act applies to recorded sound, illegality and inadmissibility can travel together.
Courts also disagreed for decades about one spouse recording another at home. The 5th Circuit created an interspousal exception in Simpson v. Simpson in 1974, but most circuits rejected it, including the 10th in Heggy v. Heggy in 1988. The 11th Circuit overruled its inherited exception in 2003, leaving the Simpson ruling a conspicuous outlier.
A robot vacuum adds another twist: The Wiretap Act covers intercepted sound, not silent video. Camera-only recording therefore falls outside that federal regime. Liability and admissibility then depend on state laws that differ sharply in scope, consent requirements and penalties.
Third is reliability. Consumer devices were designed to clean floors, not withstand cross-examination; timestamps, firmware changes and retention policies can complicate interpretation. A remote-access log may identify an account without proving who used it.
Lawyers in the Dabate case challenged the Fitbit evidence on reliability grounds, although the court upheld its admission after expert review. Each new device category raises similar questions. Examiners need validated methods to acquire, authenticate and interpret data, as the Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence recommends for novel devices.
Charting a path forward
Consumers would have a better idea of their exposure if manufacturers disclosed at the point of sale what a device records, where the data goes and how long it persists. Federal trade regulators already urge clear prepurchase disclosures and data minimization for connected products. Those principles could be applied to remote viewing, not remain buried in terms of service agreements.
It would also help if manufacturers provided exportable logs showing when remote access occurred, which account connected and whether the camera or microphone was active. Federal vehicle event-data rules offer a model by standardizing records and retrieval. Existing internet-connected device guidance supports trustworthy time references, alteration protections, access controls and defined retention.
Legislatures could address intimate surveillance directly to prevent the current patchwork of laws from punishing betrayed spouses, enabling abusers and guiding neither clearly. Funding agencies and standards bodies could prioritize consumer-device forensics so that courts admit evidence because it is validated, not merely because it looks precise.
The vacuum in Taiwan did, in support of its primary function, exactly what it was designed to do: watch a room and report to the person holding the phone. The family and courts then improvised around evidentiary power that nobody had planned for. Congress and the states will need to decide what home robots may record, who may use the recordings and what they prove before words and actions in more homes end up as evidence in court.
￼
The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
Laws against surreptitiously recording someone extend to home devices like robot vacuums, but those recordings can still be used against you in court.
items.titleTR: Your robotic vacuum is a witness: What home robots mean for evidence, privacy and the law

slots.packetSpot:
Connected home devices generate an unexpected amount of data in private spaces. Regarding Meta's Muse assistant, Jason Aten said he was confronted with questions about a Messages conversation he said he had not granted permission to access; while Muse explained this through notification previews, Meta's David Singleton said message data is synced only after the user has specifically granted permission and that the assistant had misrepresented how it works.

On smart televisions, tracking viewing habits through automatic content recognition stands out as a common practice. Some of the claims concerning recording, monitoring and remote takeover of LG devices, however, are based on speculation or require the exploitation of a security vulnerability.

In Taiwan, footage taken from a robot vacuum's live camera was used both in a compensation ruling and led to the punishment of the husband who made the recording without consent. In the United States, Amazon Echo, smart meter, Fitbit and pacemaker data have also arisen in different investigations and lawsuits: the charge against James Bates was dropped; in Richard Dabate's case, the reliability of Fitbit data was accepted after expert examination; while in Ross Compton's pacemaker data, the reasonableness of the search warrant and remote access was debated. Questions remain open over consent, who obtained the records and how, whether the data was altered, and what it can actually prove.
slots.packetTitle: Traces leaking from within the home

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Jonathan Brady/PA Images
As the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI) sweep across the labour force, it’s understandable for workers to be concerned about which jobs are most at risk of being replaced by technology.
Women make up the majority of workers in the care sector where human interactions matter most – child care, nursing and aged care. So, policymakers might reasonably presume that women’s jobs are largely shielded from the impacts of AI.
But our analysis of recent data from government agency Jobs and Skills Australia shows that it’s actually female-concentrated segments of the workforce that are most exposed to AI-fuelled automation.
Which jobs are most at risk?
The agency calculated an “automation exposure score” for every occupation in the workforce, measuring the potential for a worker’s tasks to be done by AI technologies.
Clerical and administrative jobs are among those with the highest automation exposure scores. This aligns with economists’ expectations that AI is well suited to alleviate human effort for repetitive routine tasks.
Yet this sector, which is highly exposed to automation, is also more than 70% female and provides almost one in five jobs for all women in the Australian workforce.
This gender pattern shows up when we look at the 20 top occupations most at risk of automation. 15 of these jobs are female-dominated. Of these, five would be classified as highly female-dominated, comprised of at least 80% women.
Secretaries, receptionists, bookkeepers, and accounting, human resources and payroll clerks are all among these top 20 occupations most at risk of being displaced by automation.

Only one occupation on this top 20 list is moderately male dominated: financial dealers. The remaining four are gender-balanced.
Contrast this to the 20 occupations that are least exposed to automation. Seventeen of these are male-dominated. Female-concentrated jobs make up just three of these jobs most sheltered from being displaced by AI.

Is AI already replacing these jobs?
A slowdown in job vacancy numbers could signal that these effects of AI are being felt in the economy.
Internet job vacancy data, also collected by Jobs and Skills Australia, shows that vacancies for many of these jobs highly exposed to automation have been shrinking over the past three years. And by a larger magnitude than the slowdown across the wider workforce.
For instance, vacancies for personal assistants and bookkeepers for the month of June 2026 were around 22% lower than at the same time a year earlier. Openings for general clerks were down by around 9%.
By comparison, total workforce vacancies were only around 1.7% weaker.
Among the occupations less exposed to AI, vacancies for concreters were up by 5.5%, while electricians were up by 14.3%.

At this stage, trades and labourer jobs are less exposed to automation. These hands-on jobs still require human judgement and dexterity to navigate physical conditions that can be unpredictable and differ site by site.
Checking for blind spots
All kinds of groups – tech companies, governments, education providers and researchers – are trying to predict how AI will disrupt different jobs across the workforce.
Our analysis shows that unless we intentionally apply a gender lens, we could end up ignoring gender patterns in AI’s impacts.
The federal government already requires all new policy proposals to undergo a gender analysis. This requirement should therefore also apply to policies and decisions by the newly announced Office of AI.
In particular, applying a gender lens can inform the design of policies to support the labour market’s adaptation to and adoption of AI.
This puts us on the front foot to design smart policies to proactively address AI’s disruption, instead of waiting to respond after the fallout.
For instance, having detected the higher risk of these heavily female jobs to AI automation, we can set up systems to recognise the skills of clerical and administrative workers that can be easily transferred, to match them to new opportunities.
This could include the new and emerging jobs being created by AI, as well as human-centered jobs and tasks requiring critical judgement that AI can’t replace.
Applying this gender lens to Australia’s AI policies will support a dynamic, adaptive labour market hand-in-hand with a gender equitable economy.
￼
Leonora Risse receives research funding from the Trawalla Foundation and the Women's Leadership Institute Australia. She serves as an Expert Panel Member for the Fair Work Commission and the Parliamentary Budget Office. She formerly served on the Jobs and Skills Australia Advisory Panel for the Gender Economic Equality Study.
Elise Stephenson receives research funding from the Australian Research Council (DE250100718), the Australian Government, and the Women's Leadership Institute of Australia. She is currently supporting the work of the Victorian Women's Trust (VWT) on gendered harms of AI through VWT's Feminist Researcher in Residence program.
Of the top 20 occupations most at risk of being automated, 15 are dominated by women.
